Proposition 39 : Voter ID for in-person and mail voting
Published September 29, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026
Proposition 39 would require voters to show government-issued ID to vote in person. To vote by mail, voters would have to pick a government ID number for their registration and write its last four digits on each ballot envelope, and ballots would not count if the number does not match. It would also require elections officials to try to verify voters' citizenship and report on it each year, and the state to offer a free voter ID card.
Summary by CityHallPass , not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: California Official Voter Information Guide: Proposition 39 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/).
Results
Polls close at 8 p.m. Pacific on Nov. 3. First results appear here after that.
At a glance
Proposition 39
Voting in person Show government-issued ID every time
Voting by mail Write the last four digits of the ID number you chose at registration; no match, no count
Free voter ID card The state must provide one on request
Cost Tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars a year, state and local (Legislative Analyst)
LA County voters who used vote centers, Nov. 2024 1,060,354 of 3,793,106 (27.95%)
Money raised, through Nov. 1, 2026 For: $33.0 million (one committee). Against: $33.3 million (three committees, net of transfers)
Largest donor For: Richard Uihlein, $17 million. Against: California Democratic Party, $7.3 million to the three No committees
Latest public poll PPIC, Oct. 16-22: 41% yes, 58% no (likely voters)
Each figure is sourced in the sections below. Money figures are our totals from the committees' state campaign reports, including late contribution reports filed through Nov. 1.
Details and source links: Polls , Money for and against , What it costs , Sources .
What does a yes vote on Proposition 39 mean?
Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote.
What does a no vote on Proposition 39 mean?
A voter's identity would continue to be established with the voter's signature.
What would Proposition 39 cost?
The Legislative Analyst estimates state and local costs of tens of millions of dollars to low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to put the new requirements in place. The amount depends on later decisions, such as how the free ID card is designed and how many people request one.
What it means for the City of LA
The ID rules would apply to every election in California, including City of Los Angeles elections, which the County of Los Angeles now runs for the City. State law today bars cities from requiring voter ID; Proposition 39 would write the requirement into the State Constitution. The Legislative Analyst estimates state and local costs of tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars a year but gives no figure for the City. The City's proposed 2026-27 budget sets aside $11 million for its general municipal elections.
The details
Official title Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Type Initiative constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by petition signatures
Votes needed to pass Simple majority (more than 50% yes) of votes cast statewide
The question on your ballot
Invalidates mail ballots that do not have last four digits of designated government-issued identification number written on envelope. Prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Fiscal Impact: Costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements. Supporters: The Transparency Foundation; Latino American Political Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; CA Women’s Leadership Assn Opponents: ACLU California Action; Common Cause; League of Women Voters of California
What would change
Today If Proposition 39 passes
Proving who you are when you register Voters give a driver’s license number, state ID number or the last four digits of their Social Security number. Those who do not may be asked for ID the first time they vote (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)) Same, and each voter must also designate one government-issued ID for voting (text, Art. II, Sec. 3.1(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Voting in person Voters sign a roster. Officials generally do not verify those signatures before counting (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)) Voters must show government-issued ID every time (text, Sec. 3.1(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Voting by mail Voters sign the envelope, and officials check the signature before counting (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)) Voters also write the last four digits of their designated ID number. A ballot counts only after officials verify the number matches (text, Sec. 3.1(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)). If a voter uses a different ID’s number than the one designated, the ballot would not count (Attorney General’s summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/title-summary.htm))
Citizenship Voters attest to citizenship under penalty of perjury when they register (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)) The Secretary of State and county officials must use “best efforts” with government data to verify citizenship and report each year the share of each county’s rolls verified (text, Sec. 3.1(a) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Free ID Not applicable The state must give a voter ID card at no charge to any eligible voter who asks (text, Sec. 3.1(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Audits Not applicable The State Auditor audits the state’s and each county’s compliance every odd-numbered year (text, Sec. 3.1(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Which elections Not applicable “Any election in the State” (text, Sec. 3.1(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
The measure does not say which IDs count. It defines government-issued ID only as documentation “that allows conclusive verification of the voter’s identity” (text, Sec. 3.1(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)). The Legislative Analyst says the Legislature would have to pass laws to settle which forms of ID are accepted and what counts as “best efforts” on citizenship (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)). The measure does not repeal signature checks on mail ballots.
What it would mean for City of Los Angeles elections
It would cover City elections. The ID rule applies to “any election in the State” (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)), and the Legislative Analyst says each ballot cast “in any election in California” would need the added ID information (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)).
The County runs them. City elections for Mayor, Council, other City offices and City measures are held in even-numbered years. Since 2020 the County of Los Angeles has run most of the work of those elections (City Clerk (https://clerk.lacity.gov/elections)).
Today a city cannot require ID. A 2024 state law bars any city, including a charter city, from requiring ID to vote “unless required by state or federal law” (Elections Code Sec. 10005, SB 1174 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SB1174)). Courts blocked Huntington Beach’s voter-approved voter ID charter amendment, and in January 2026 the State Supreme Court declined to review the appeals court ruling (Orange County Register (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/01/29/california-supreme-court-wont-review-huntington-beachs-voter-id-law-leaving-appeals-court-decision-against-the-city/)). Proposition 39 would put the requirement in the State Constitution.
How Angelenos vote now. In the November 2024 election, 2,732,752 of the 3,793,106 Los Angeles County ballots (72.05%) were cast by mail and 1,060,354 (27.95%) at vote centers (LA County Registrar (https://results.lavote.gov/text-results/4324)). Under Prop. 39, the first group would add ID digits to the envelope and the second would show ID.
Rejected mail ballots in LA County. In November 2024 the County rejected 21,356 of 2,764,734 returned mail ballots (0.77%), including 7,967 for signatures that did not match and 3,272 with no signature (Secretary of State (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/vbm-rejection-reason/2024/november-general-2024.pdf)). In the June 2026 primary it rejected 24,806 (1.34%), including 7,190 for mismatched signatures (Secretary of State (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/vbm-rejection-reason/2026/june-primary-2026.pdf)).
Cost. The Legislative Analyst estimates state and local costs of tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars a year and gives no figure for any one city or county (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)). The City’s proposed 2026-27 budget holds $11 million for general municipal election expenses, up from $10 million in 2025-26 (CAO, Unappropriated Balance (https://cao.lacity.gov/content/budget/26-27/2026-27ProposedBudget.pdf#page=255)).
Neighborhood Council elections. The City Clerk runs Neighborhood Council elections in odd-numbered years (City Clerk (https://clerk.lacity.gov/elections)). Voters in them need not be U.S. citizens, and the voting age is 16 (EmpowerLA (https://neighborhoodempowerment.lacity.gov/elections/)). Neither the measure nor the Legislative Analyst says whether these elections would count as an “election in the State” for the ID rule.
Timing. The Nov. 3, 2026 election, with the City’s Mayor race (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/races/mayor) and eight City measures (City Clerk list (https://cityclerk.lacity.org/onlinedocs/2026/26-1100-S8_misc_08-03-26.pdf)), runs under current rules, since an approved amendment takes effect only after the vote is certified (Cal. Const., Art. XVIII, Sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)). Under the City’s even-year schedule, the next regular City election would be in 2028 (City Clerk (https://clerk.lacity.gov/elections)).
How it got on the ballot
Proposition 39 is a citizen initiative, placed on the ballot by voter petitions.
Sept. 19, 2025: The Attorney General issued the petition’s title and summary. The proponents are Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, Sen. Tony Strickland and Donald J. DiCostanzo (Secretary of State, eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)). LAist describes DeMaio and Strickland as the two Republican legislators behind it (LAist (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-proposition-39)).
Oct. 21, 2025: The campaign reported gathering 25% of the signatures needed (Secretary of State, eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)).
March 2026: Petitions were filed with the counties. They held 1,367,961 raw signatures, 264,563 of them from Los Angeles County (Secretary of State random sample count (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/1984-finalrandomsample-04-24-26.pdf)). That is about 19% from Los Angeles County (our calculation).
April 24, 2026: The random sample projected 1,027,018 valid signatures, more than 110% of the 874,641 needed, and the measure became eligible (Secretary of State random sample count (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/1984-finalrandomsample-04-24-26.pdf)).
Title change (July-Aug. 2026): Voters had signed the petition under the title “Establishes Additional Voter Identification and Citizenship Verification Requirements” (Secretary of State, eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)). The ballot title is “Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification” (guide (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/title-summary.htm)). The Yes campaign sued over the new title. On Aug. 6, Sacramento Superior Court Judge Jennifer K. Rockwell ruled that the title, summary and label “accurately describe the effect of the measure.” In a separate suit by Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas and Senate President pro Tem Monique Limón, Judge Shelleyanne Chang tentatively found misleading the Yes argument’s claim that the measure would make voting easier (LA Times (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-08-07/judge-rejects-challenge-to-california-attorney-generals-description-of-voter-id-measure); Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/08/03/california-voter-id-prop-39-both-sides-sue/)).
Vote needed. As a constitutional amendment, it passes with a majority of votes cast statewide (Cal. Const., Art. XVIII, Sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)).
What each side says
In the state voter guide. Arguments are the opinions of their authors and have not been checked for accuracy by any official agency (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument for, signed by the Democratic, Republican and Independent coalition chairs of Californians for Voter ID, Margit Whitlock, Tafa Jefferson and Joe Green (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
Trust: voter ID is “a common-sense reform to increase trust and participation.”
Access: mail ballots and extended hours stay, and every voter can get a free ID.
Signatures: “In the last election, more than 100,000 ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches.”
Turnout: states with voter ID and free IDs have “seen an increase in voting.”
Audits: an independent audit every two years and citizenship checks of the rolls.
The opponents’ rebuttal, signed by U.S. Sen. Alex Padilla, the California Nurses Association and the California School Employees Association, says the measure is funded by “MAGA rightwing billionaires,” that Texas threw out “12 times more mail ballots than California” under similar rules, and that the Legislative Analyst found it could cost “hundreds of millions each year” (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument against, signed by David Trujillo of ACLU California Action, Darius Kemp of Common Cause and Lorrel Plimier of the League of Women Voters of California (argument against (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
Motive: it ties the measure to President Trump’s claims about elections.
Cost: “hundreds of millions of dollars.”
Privacy: writing ID digits on the envelope exposes voters to identity theft.
Rejected ballots: one wrong digit, an outdated address or a changed name could cause a valid ballot to be rejected, and voters who do not designate an ID “may not get a mail ballot at all.”
Hidden costs: a “free” ID still costs travel, time off and documents.
The supporters’ rebuttal, signed by the Transparency Foundation, the California Women’s Leadership Association and the Latino American Political Association, says the measure “is not about Donald Trump or Gavin Newsom” and that “states with voter ID laws have not seen decreases in voter participation” (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Outside the guide.
California Republican Party Chair Corrin Rankin: “ID is required for so many things that we do in life” (ABC7 (https://abc7.com/post/what-know-proposition-39-californias-voter-id-measure/19872464/)).
Democratic candidate for governor Xavier Becerra said a voter who registered under a maiden name and votes under a married name could have the vote blocked (ABC7 (https://abc7.com/post/what-know-proposition-39-californias-voter-id-measure/19872464/)).
DeMaio called it a “superior model” to the federal SAVE America Act because it keeps mail voting (Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/08/03/california-voter-id-prop-39-both-sides-sue/)).
LA County Supervisor Holly Mitchell: “LA County’s elections are already secure, and Prop 39 does nothing to make them safer” (City News Service via Westside Current (https://www.westsidecurrent.com/county_news/county-leaders-enter-the-fight-over-proposed-voter-id-laws/article_de479320-c977-4c0a-8545-822fee0f22b6.html)).
County registrars interviewed by ABC7 said checking partial ID numbers could take longer than signature checks (ABC7 (https://abc7.com/post/what-know-proposition-39-californias-voter-id-measure/19872464/)).

## Proposition 39: Requires government-issued identification to vote
Proposition 39 would amend the state Constitution to introduce new voter ID requirements for in-person and mail voting.
The measure would prohibit citizens from voting in elections unless they present government-issued identification that matches their voter registration.
The measure also includes requirements for election officials related to verifying citizenship.
A yes vote would establish the proposed identification and verification requirements.
A no vote would leave existing election rules in place.
Supporters say the measure would strengthen election security and increase public confidence in voting.
Opponents argue that the requirements could create barriers for eligible voters who lack the required documents and that existing safeguards already protect election integrity.

Proposition 39 : Voter ID for in-person and mail voting
Published September 29, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026
Proposition 39 would require voters to show government-issued ID to vote in person. To vote by mail, voters would have to pick a government ID number for their registration and write its last four digits on each ballot envelope, and ballots would not count if the number does not match. It would also require elections officials to try to verify voters' citizenship and report on it each year, and the state to offer a free voter ID card.
Summary by CityHallPass , not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: California Official Voter Information Guide: Proposition 39 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/).

What does a yes vote on Proposition 39 mean?
Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote.
What does a no vote on Proposition 39 mean?
A voter's identity would continue to be established with the voter's signature.
What would Proposition 39 cost?
The Legislative Analyst estimates state and local costs of tens of millions of dollars to low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to put the new requirements in place. The amount depends on later decisions, such as how the free ID card is designed and how many people request one.
What it means for the City of LA
The ID rules would apply to every election in California, including City of Los Angeles elections, which the County of Los Angeles now runs for the City. State law today bars cities from requiring voter ID; Proposition 39 would write the requirement into the State Constitution. The Legislative Analyst estimates state and local costs of tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars a year but gives no figure for the City. The City's proposed 2026-27 budget sets aside $11 million for its general municipal elections.

Officials generally do not verify those signatures before counting (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)) Voters must show government-issued ID every time (text, Sec. 3.1(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Voting by mail Voters sign the envelope, and officials check the signature before counting (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)) Voters also write the last four digits of their designated ID number. A ballot counts only after officials verify the number matches (text, Sec. 3.1(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)). If a voter uses a different ID’s number than the one designated, the ballot would not count (Attorney General’s summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/title-summary.htm))

It defines government-issued ID only as documentation “that allows conclusive verification of the voter’s identity” (text, Sec. 3.1(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)). The County runs them. City elections for Mayor, Council, other City offices and City measures are held in even-numbered years. Since 2020 the County of Los Angeles has run most of the work of those elections (City Clerk (https://clerk.lacity.gov/elections)).

How Angelenos vote now. In the November 2024 election, 2,732,752 of the 3,793,106 Los Angeles County ballots (72.05%) were cast by mail and 1,060,354 (27.95%) at vote centers (LA County Registrar (https://results.lavote.gov/text-results/4324)). Cost. The Legislative Analyst estimates state and local costs of tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars a year and gives no figure for any one city or county (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)). The City’s proposed 2026-27 budget holds $11 million for general municipal election expenses, up from $10 million in 2025-26 (CAO, Unappropriated Balance (https://cao.lacity.gov/content/budget/26-27/2026-27ProposedBudget.pdf#page=255)).

Voters in them need not be U.S. citizens, and the voting age is 16 (EmpowerLA (https://neighborhoodempowerment.lacity.gov/elections/)). Neither the measure nor the Legislative Analyst says whether these elections would count as an “election in the State” for the ID rule.

The Nov. 3, 2026 election, with the City’s Mayor race (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/races/mayor) and eight City measures (City Clerk list (https://cityclerk.lacity.org/onlinedocs/2026/26-1100-S8_misc_08-03-26.pdf)), runs under current rules, since an approved amendment takes effect only after the vote is certified (Cal. Const., Art. XVIII, Sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)). Vote needed. As a constitutional amendment, it passes with a majority of votes cast statewide (Cal. Const., Art. XVIII, Sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)).

Proposition 39 : Voter ID for in-person and mail voting
Published September 29, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026
Proposition 39 would require voters to show government-issued ID to vote in person. To vote by mail, voters would have to pick a government ID number for their registration and write its last four digits on each ballot envelope, and ballots would not count if the number does not match. It would also require elections officials to try to verify voters' citizenship and report on it each year, and the state to offer a free voter ID card.

What does a yes vote on Proposition 39 mean?
Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote.
What does a no vote on Proposition 39 mean?
A voter's identity would continue to be established with the voter's signature.
What would Proposition 39 cost?
The Legislative Analyst estimates state and local costs of tens of millions of dollars to low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to put the new requirements in place. The amount depends on later decisions, such as how the free ID card is designed and how many people request one.

The ID rules would apply to every election in California, including City of Los Angeles elections, which the County of Los Angeles now runs for the City. State law today bars cities from requiring voter ID; Proposition 39 would write the requirement into the State Constitution. The Legislative Analyst estimates state and local costs of tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars a year but gives no figure for the City. The City's proposed 2026-27 budget sets aside $11 million for its general municipal elections.

Rockwell ruled that the title, summary and label “accurately describe the effect of the measure.” In a separate suit by Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas and Senate President pro Tem Monique Limón, Judge Shelleyanne Chang tentatively found misleading the Yes argument’s claim that the measure would make voting easier (LA Times (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-08-07/judge-rejects-challenge-to-california-attorney-generals-description-of-voter-id-measure); Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/08/03/california-voter-id-prop-39-both-sides-sue/)).
Vote needed. As a constitutional amendment, it passes with a majority of votes cast statewide (Cal. Const., Art. XVIII, Sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)).
What each side says
In the state voter guide. Arguments are the opinions of their authors and have not been checked for accuracy by any official agency (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument for, signed by the Democratic, Republican and Independent coalition chairs of Californians for Voter ID, Margit Whitlock, Tafa Jefferson and Joe Green (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
Trust: voter ID is “a common-sense reform to increase trust and participation.”
Access: mail ballots and extended hours stay, and every voter can get a free ID.
Signatures: “In the last election, more than 100,000 ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches.”
Turnout: states with voter ID and free IDs have “seen an increase in voting.”
Audits: an independent audit every two years and citizenship checks of the rolls.
The opponents’ rebuttal, signed by U.S. Sen. Alex Padilla, the California Nurses Association and the California School Employees Association, says the measure is funded by “MAGA rightwing billionaires,” that Texas threw out “12 times more mail ballots than California” under similar rules, and that the Legislative Analyst found it could cost “hundreds of millions each year” (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument against, signed by David Trujillo of ACLU California Action, Darius Kemp of Common Cause and Lorrel Plimier of the League of Women Voters of California (argument against (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
Motive: it ties the measure to President Trump’s claims about elections.
Cost: “hundreds of millions of dollars.”
Privacy: writing ID digits on the envelope exposes voters to identity theft.
Rejected ballots: one wrong digit, an outdated address or a changed name could cause a valid ballot to be rejected, and voters who do not designate an ID “may not get a mail ballot at all.”
Hidden costs: a “free” ID still costs travel, time off and documents.
The supporters’ rebuttal, signed by the Transparency Foundation, the California Women’s Leadership Association and the Latino American Political Association, says the measure “is not about Donald Trump or Gavin Newsom” and that “states with voter ID laws have not seen decreases in voter participation” (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Outside the guide.
California Republican Party Chair Corrin Rankin: “ID is required for so many things that we do in life” (ABC7 (https://abc7.com/post/what-know-proposition-39-californias-voter-id-measure/19872464/)).
Democratic candidate for governor Xavier Becerra said a voter who registered under a maiden name and votes under a married name could have the vote blocked (ABC7 (https://abc7.com/post/what-know-proposition-39-californias-voter-id-measure/19872464/)).
DeMaio called it a “superior model” to the federal SAVE America Act because it keeps mail voting (Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/08/03/california-voter-id-prop-39-both-sides-sue/)).
LA County Supervisor Holly Mitchell: “LA County’s elections are already secure, and Prop 39 does nothing to make them safer” (City News Service via Westside Current (https://www.westsidecurrent.com/county_news/county-leaders-enter-the-fight-over-proposed-voter-id-laws/article_de479320-c977-4c0a-8545-822fee0f22b6.html)).
County registrars interviewed by ABC7 said checking partial ID numbers could take longer than signature checks (ABC7 (https://abc7.com/post/what-know-proposition-39-californias-voter-id-measure/19872464/)).
Checking the main factual claims against official records.
Claim Who makes it What official records show
More than 100,000 ballots were rejected for signature mismatches “in the last election” Yes campaign The argument does not name the election. Statewide, 71,387 mail ballots were rejected for non-matching signatures in November 2024 and 43,976 in the June 2026 primary (Secretary of State, Nov. 2024 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/vbm-rejection-reason/2024/november-general-2024.pdf); June 2026 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/vbm-rejection-reason/2026/june-primary-2026.pdf)). We did not find a statewide election with more than 100,000
Voter ID would replace slow signature checks Yes campaign (implied) The measure adds ID digits and does not repeal signature checks (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)). Rivas and Limón made the same point in court (Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/08/03/california-voter-id-prop-39-both-sides-sue/))

Proposition 39 would amend the state Constitution to introduce new voter ID requirements for in-person and mail voting.

Proposition 39 : Voter ID for in-person and mail voting
Published September 29, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026
Proposition 39 would require voters to show government-issued ID to vote in person. To vote by mail, voters would have to pick a government ID number for their registration and write its last four digits on each ballot envelope, and ballots would not count if the number does not match. It would also require elections officials to try to verify voters' citizenship and report on it each year, and the state to offer a free voter ID card.
Summary by CityHallPass , not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: California Official Voter Information Guide: Proposition 39 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/).

What does a yes vote on Proposition 39 mean?
Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote.
What does a no vote on Proposition 39 mean?
A voter's identity would continue to be established with the voter's signature.
What would Proposition 39 cost?
The Legislative Analyst estimates state and local costs of tens of millions of dollars to low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to put the new requirements in place. The amount depends on later decisions, such as how the free ID card is designed and how many people request one.
What it means for the City of LA
The ID rules would apply to every election in California, including City of Los Angeles elections, which the County of Los Angeles now runs for the City. State law today bars cities from requiring voter ID; Proposition 39 would write the requirement into the State Constitution. The Legislative Analyst estimates state and local costs of tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars a year but gives no figure for the City. The City's proposed 2026-27 budget sets aside $11 million for its general municipal elections.
The details
Official title Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Type Initiative constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by petition signatures
Votes needed to pass Simple majority (more than 50% yes) of votes cast statewide
The question on your ballot
Invalidates mail ballots that do not have last four digits of designated government-issued identification number written on envelope. Prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Fiscal Impact: Costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements. Supporters: The Transparency Foundation; Latino American Political Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; CA Women’s Leadership Assn Opponents: ACLU California Action; Common Cause; League of Women Voters of California
What would change
Today If Proposition 39 passes
Proving who you are when you register Voters give a driver’s license number, state ID number or the last four digits of their Social Security number. Those who do not may be asked for ID the first time they vote (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)) Same, and each voter must also designate one government-issued ID for voting (text, Art. II, Sec. 3.1(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Voting in person Voters sign a roster. Officials generally do not verify those signatures before counting (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)) Voters must show government-issued ID every time (text, Sec. 3.1(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Voting by mail Voters sign the envelope, and officials check the signature before counting (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)) Voters also write the last four digits of their designated ID number. A ballot counts only after officials verify the number matches (text, Sec. 3.1(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)). If a voter uses a different ID’s number than the one designated, the ballot would not count (Attorney General’s summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/title-summary.htm))
Citizenship Voters attest to citizenship under penalty of perjury when they register (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)) The Secretary of State and county officials must use “best efforts” with government data to verify citizenship and report each year the share of each county’s rolls verified (text, Sec. 3.1(a) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Free ID Not applicable The state must give a voter ID card at no charge to any eligible voter who asks (text, Sec. 3.1(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Audits Not applicable The State Auditor audits the state’s and each county’s compliance every odd-numbered year (text, Sec. 3.1(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Which elections Not applicable “Any election in the State” (text, Sec. 3.1(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
The measure does not say which IDs count. It defines government-issued ID only as documentation “that allows conclusive verification of the voter’s identity” (text, Sec. 3.1(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)). The Legislative Analyst says the Legislature would have to pass laws to settle which forms of ID are accepted and what counts as “best efforts” on citizenship (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)). The measure does not repeal signature checks on mail ballots.
What it would mean for City of Los Angeles elections
It would cover City elections. The ID rule applies to “any election in the State” (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)), and the Legislative Analyst says each ballot cast “in any election in California” would need the added ID information (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)).
The County runs them. City elections for Mayor, Council, other City offices and City measures are held in even-numbered years. Since 2020 the County of Los Angeles has run most of the work of those elections (City Clerk (https://clerk.lacity.gov/elections)).
Today a city cannot require ID. A 2024 state law bars any city, including a charter city, from requiring ID to vote “unless required by state or federal law” (Elections Code Sec. 10005, SB 1174 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SB1174)). Courts blocked Huntington Beach’s voter-approved voter ID charter amendment, and in January 2026 the State Supreme Court declined to review the appeals court ruling (Orange County Register (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/01/29/california-supreme-court-wont-review-huntington-beachs-voter-id-law-leaving-appeals-court-decision-against-the-city/)). Proposition 39 would put the requirement in the State Constitution.
How Angelenos vote now. In the November 2024 election, 2,732,752 of the 3,793,106 Los Angeles County ballots (72.05%) were cast by mail and 1,060,354 (27.95%) at vote centers (LA County Registrar (https://results.lavote.gov/text-results/4324)). Under Prop. 39, the first group would add ID digits to the envelope and the second would show ID.
Rejected mail ballots in LA County. In November 2024 the County rejected 21,356 of 2,764,734 returned mail ballots (0.77%), including 7,967 for signatures that did not match and 3,272 with no signature (Secretary of State (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/vbm-rejection-reason/2024/november-general-2024.pdf)). In the June 2026 primary it rejected 24,806 (1.34%), including 7,190 for mismatched signatures (Secretary of State (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/vbm-rejection-reason/2026/june-primary-2026.pdf)).
Cost. The Legislative Analyst estimates state and local costs of tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars a year and gives no figure for any one city or county (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)). The City’s proposed 2026-27 budget holds $11 million for general municipal election expenses, up from $10 million in 2025-26 (CAO, Unappropriated Balance (https://cao.lacity.gov/content/budget/26-27/2026-27ProposedBudget.pdf#page=255)).
Neighborhood Council elections. The City Clerk runs Neighborhood Council elections in odd-numbered years (City Clerk (https://clerk.lacity.gov/elections)). Voters in them need not be U.S. citizens, and the voting age is 16 (EmpowerLA (https://neighborhoodempowerment.lacity.gov/elections/)). Neither the measure nor the Legislative Analyst says whether these elections would count as an “election in the State” for the ID rule.
Timing. The Nov. 3, 2026 election, with the City’s Mayor race (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/races/mayor) and eight City measures (City Clerk list (https://cityclerk.lacity.org/onlinedocs/2026/26-1100-S8_misc_08-03-26.pdf)), runs under current rules, since an approved amendment takes effect only after the vote is certified (Cal. Const., Art. XVIII, Sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)). Under the City’s even-year schedule, the next regular City election would be in 2028 (City Clerk (https://clerk.lacity.gov/elections)).
How it got on the ballot
Proposition 39 is a citizen initiative, placed on the ballot by voter petitions.
Sept. 19, 2025: The Attorney General issued the petition’s title and summary. The proponents are Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, Sen. Tony Strickland and Donald J. DiCostanzo (Secretary of State, eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)). LAist describes DeMaio and Strickland as the two Republican legislators behind it (LAist (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-proposition-39)).
Oct. 21, 2025: The campaign reported gathering 25% of the signatures needed (Secretary of State, eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)).
March 2026: Petitions were filed with the counties. They held 1,367,961 raw signatures, 264,563 of them from Los Angeles County (Secretary of State random sample count (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/1984-finalrandomsample-04-24-26.pdf)). That is about 19% from Los Angeles County (our calculation).
April 24, 2026: The random sample projected 1,027,018 valid signatures, more than 110% of the 874,641 needed, and the measure became eligible (Secretary of State random sample count (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/1984-finalrandomsample-04-24-26.pdf)).
Title change (July-Aug. 2026): Voters had signed the petition under the title “Establishes Additional Voter Identification and Citizenship Verification Requirements” (Secretary of State, eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)). The ballot title is “Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification” (guide (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/title-summary.htm)). The Yes campaign sued over the new title. On Aug. 6, Sacramento Superior Court Judge Jennifer K. Rockwell ruled that the title, summary and label “accurately describe the effect of the measure.” In a separate suit by Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas and Senate President pro Tem Monique Limón, Judge Shelleyanne Chang tentatively found misleading the Yes argument’s claim that the measure would make voting easier (LA Times (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-08-07/judge-rejects-challenge-to-california-attorney-generals-description-of-voter-id-measure); Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/08/03/california-voter-id-prop-39-both-sides-sue/)).
Vote needed. As a constitutional amendment, it passes with a majority of votes cast statewide (Cal. Const., Art. XVIII, Sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)).
What each side says
In the state voter guide. Arguments are the opinions of their authors and have not been checked for accuracy by any official agency (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument for, signed by the Democratic, Republican and Independent coalition chairs of Californians for Voter ID, Margit Whitlock, Tafa Jefferson and Joe Green (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
Trust: voter ID is “a common-sense reform to increase trust and participation.”
Access: mail ballots and extended hours stay, and every voter can get a free ID.
Signatures: “In the last election, more than 100,000 ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches.”
Turnout: states with voter ID and free IDs have “seen an increase in voting.”
Audits: an independent audit every two years and citizenship checks of the rolls.
The opponents’ rebuttal, signed by U.S. Sen. Alex Padilla, the California Nurses Association and the California School Employees Association, says the measure is funded by “MAGA rightwing billionaires,” that Texas threw out “12 times more mail ballots than California” under similar rules, and that the Legislative Analyst found it could cost “hundreds of millions each year” (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument against, signed by David Trujillo of ACLU California Action, Darius Kemp of Common Cause and Lorrel Plimier of the League of Women Voters of California (argument against (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
Motive: it ties the measure to President Trump’s claims about elections.
Cost: “hundreds of millions of dollars.”
Privacy: writing ID digits on the envelope exposes voters to identity theft.
Rejected ballots: one wrong digit, an outdated address or a changed name could cause a valid ballot to be rejected, and voters who do not designate an ID “may not get a mail ballot at all.”
Hidden costs: a “free” ID still costs travel, time off and documents.
The supporters’ rebuttal, signed by the Transparency Foundation, the California Women’s Leadership Association and the Latino American Political Association, says the measure “is not about Donald Trump or Gavin Newsom” and that “states with voter ID laws have not seen decreases in voter participation” (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Outside the guide.
California Republican Party Chair Corrin Rankin: “ID is required for so many things that we do in life” (ABC7 (https://abc7.com/post/what-know-proposition-39-californias-voter-id-measure/19872464/)).
Democratic candidate for governor Xavier Becerra said a voter who registered under a maiden name and votes under a married name could have the vote blocked (ABC7 (https://abc7.com/post/what-know-proposition-39-californias-voter-id-measure/19872464/)).
DeMaio called it a “superior model” to the federal SAVE America Act because it keeps mail voting (Mercury News (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/08/03/california-voter-id-prop-39-both-sides-sue/)).
LA County Supervisor Holly Mitchell: “LA County’s elections are already secure, and Prop 39 does nothing to make them safer” (City News Service via Westside Current (https://www.westsidecurrent.com/county_news/county-leaders-enter-the-fight-over-proposed-voter-id-laws/article_de479320-c977-4c0a-8545-822fee0f22b6.html)).
County registrars interviewed by ABC7 said checking partial ID numbers could take longer than signature checks (ABC7 (https://abc7.com/post/what-know-proposition-39-californias-voter-id-measure/19872464/)).

- The measure does NOT repeal signature checks — so it adds a layer, not replaces.
- LAO: costs tens of millions to low hundreds of millions per year.
- Maryland study: ~2.7 million Californians (11% of eligible voters) lack a driver's license; 13% have expired/outdated; 24% lack a passport; 3M+ would have difficulty accessing citizenship documents.
- Private right of action → litigation risk.
- Texas SB 1 experience: mail ballot rejection went from <1% to >12% in the 2022 primary.
- Funding: Yes $36.5M mostly from out-of-state billionaire Richard Uihlein ($17M) and Joe Gebbia ($8M).
- No cure process specified in the text for wrong digits.
- The measure doesn't specify which IDs count.

1. The University of Maryland study on who lacks ID in California (to verify numbers).

4. Evidence on noncitizen voting in CA — the Heritage Foundation database of 71 cases 1982-2025.
5. Academic literature on strict voter ID effects on turnout, particularly on mail-in voting (e.g., Georgia's 2021 law — actually Georgia requires ID on absentee ballots since SB 202, and there were high rejection rates initially).
6. Any additional legal risk: NVRA preemption, or the fact that a constitutional amendment conflicting with federal law (HAVA/NVRA) might be unenforceable. Also potential conflict with the state constitution's "free elections" clause.
7. Also check the counterargument: some moderates/centrists support voter ID. Let me check IVN (Independent Voter Project) position — they had a poll showing 43-40 favor. Does IVN endorse yes? Let me check. Also check whether any credible nonpartisan group supports it. Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association supports it (odd, since it costs money). Also the Pasadena Star-News endorsed yes.

Let me also look at whether the measure has any provision addressing voters who lack the designated ID — the free voter ID card. And whether there's a concern about the "designate an ID at registration" step: existing voters may not have designated an ID; the measure requires new AND existing voters to select a government-issued ID in their voter registration to vote by mail. If they don't, do they get a mail ballot? The AG summary says "Invalidates mail ballots that do not have last four digits of designated government-issued identification number written on envelope." The No campaign says "if you don't take extra steps to tell officials which ID you want to use for voting—you may not get a mail ballot at all."

Let me check the Maryland study and IVN/other centrist support, plus research on voter ID turnout effects.

Very useful. Important facts confirmed:
- The Nov 3, 2026 election runs under current rules; an approved amendment takes effect only after certification. So this is about future elections.
- The Yes campaign's claim of "more than 100,000 ballots rejected due to signature mismatches" is not supported by official records (71,387 statewide in Nov 2024, 43,976 in June 2026 primary).
- A judge found Yes claims (saves money, easier to vote, privacy protections) false and misleading.
- The measure does NOT repeal signature checks — so it adds a layer, not replaces.
- LAO: costs tens of millions to low hundreds of millions per year.
- Maryland study: ~2.7 million Californians (11% of eligible voters) lack a driver's license; 13% have expired/outdated; 24% lack a passport; 3M+ would have difficulty accessing citizenship documents.
- Private right of action → litigation risk.
- Texas SB 1 experience: mail ballot rejection went from <1% to >12% in the 2022 primary.
- Funding: Yes $36.5M mostly from out-of-state billionaire Richard Uihlein ($17M) and Joe Gebbia ($8M).
- No cure process specified in the text for wrong digits.
- The measure doesn't specify which IDs count.

Let me now do a few more checks:
1. The University of Maryland study on who lacks ID in California (to verify numbers).
2. Texas SB 1 experience and peer-reviewed study on turnout.
3. Whether there is a cure process in the measure. Also — important: California already has an ID requirement for first-time voters who registered by mail without providing ID (HAVA).
4. Evidence on noncitizen voting in CA — the Heritage Foundation database of 71 cases 1982-2025.
5. Academic literature on strict voter ID effects on turnout, particularly on mail-in voting (e.g., Georgia's 2021 law — actually Georgia requires ID on absentee ballots since SB 202, and there were high rejection rates initially).
6. Any additional legal risk: NVRA preemption, or the fact that a constitutional amendment conflicting with federal law (HAVA/NVRA) might be unenforceable. Also potential conflict with the state constitution's "free elections" clause.
7. Also check the counterargument: some moderates/centrists support voter ID. Let me check IVN (Independent Voter Project) position — they had a poll showing 43-40 favor. Does IVN endorse yes? Let me check. Also check whether any credible nonpartisan group supports it. Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association supports it (odd, since it costs money). Also the Pasadena Star-News endorsed yes.

Let me also look at whether the measure has any provision addressing voters who lack the designated ID — the free voter ID card. And whether there's a concern about the "designate an ID at registration" step: existing voters may not have designated an ID; the measure requires new AND existing voters to select a government-issued ID in their voter registration to vote by mail. If they don't, do they get a mail ballot? The AG summary says "Invalidates mail ballots that do not have last four digits of designated government-issued identification number written on envelope." The No campaign says "if you don't take extra steps to tell officials which ID you want to use for voting—you may not get a mail ballot at all."

Let me check the Maryland study and IVN/other centrist support, plus research on voter ID turnout effects.

Our primary goal was to examine the extent to which adult citizens in California have the ID they might need in order to vote if California changes its voter ID law.
Since documents are not currently needed for most 
California voters when voting,2 this allows us to provide a sensitivity analysis that explores how various provisions could impact the number of people who would be able to vote with the ID they have.
We also sought to gauge Californian’s understanding of current voter ID laws, and to assess attitudes about the expense and wait time to get key documents to prove identity and citizenship in California.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first survey of voting eligible 
Californians with questions specifically about the types of identification voting eligible
Californians have.3 This research builds on national survey research conducted in 2023 and state surveys in Georgia and Texas.4

This is very relevant. Texas SB 1 is the closest analogue: requiring the ID number on the mail ballot envelope to match registration records. The result: rejection rates went from 1% (2020) to 12.38% (March 2022 primary), with 82-90% of rejections attributable to the ID number requirement. A peer-reviewed study in Journal of Politics found lasting turnout reduction — ~90% of rejected voters did not find another way to participate.

Important nuance: Texas rejection rates dropped to 2.7% within eight months as voters learned. But the DOJ is litigating under the Materiality Provision of the Civil Rights Act — arguing ID number mismatch is an "immaterial error" and thus rejection violates federal law. There's a genuine dispute; the 5th Circuit reinstated it. That's a real legal risk that Prop 39 could be blocked or litigated in federal court.

Actually, an important point: under the federal Materiality Provision (52 U.S.C. § 10101(e)), it's illegal to deny the right to vote because of an immaterial error in paperwork. Courts have split. If Prop 39 conflicts, it could be enjoined — creating chaos.

Let me also check:
1. Georgia's experience (SB 202 requires ID on absentee ballot applications).
2. Whether Prop 39 has a cure process. The text says nothing about cure — meaning a mismatch = ballot not counted. That's a big deal because California currently has robust cure rights (signature mismatch cure within 22 days).
3. Whether Prop 39 would be subject to the NVRA/HAVA. HAVA requires ID for first-time mail registrants only.

Also check the "San Francisco/Oakland noncitizen school board voting" conflict — Prop 39 requires citizenship verification for "any election in the State," which would conflict with SF and Oakland's noncitizen school board voting. Interesting: Prop 39 says officials shall verify citizenship for voter rolls. And in-person voting in "any election in the State" requires government-issued ID. This could effectively end noncitizen voting in SF/Oakland school board elections. Let me check if that's been noted.

***Requires Voters to Provide Additional Identifying Information to Vote.*** Proposition 39 requires voters to provide additional identifying information each time they cast a ballot in any election in California.
Elections officials would be required to verify voters’ identities before counting their ballots.
The identification requirement would depend on whether a voter casts their ballot in person or by mail:
- ***In-Person Voting.*** When voting in person, Proposition 39 requires voters to present government-issued identification for identity verification.
- ***Voting by Mail.*** When voting by mail, Proposition 39 requires voters to provide the last four digits of their selected government-issued identification number on the ballot envelope.
Elections officials would verify that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter’s registration information.

SAN DIEGO, Calif —California voters registered No Party Preference are not a small slice of the electorate. They account for nearly 5.3 million registered voters in the state (22.82% of the electorate), and this does not count voters registered with a party that consider themselves independent-minded.
Following a record turnout in the nonpartisan Top Two primary, largely driven by independents, it is clear these voters are not only paying attention to what is happening in their state, but they are engaged, and can reshape the California political landscape.
It’s Official: California Voters Will Decide on Billionaire Tax, Voter ID, and 12 Other Measures This November Whether the billionaire wealth tax survives will come down to a simple count: if Proposition 40 beats both Proposition 41 and Proposition 42 this November, it will stand. If either of them beats it, the tax will get erased anyway. Independent Voter News Cara Brown McCormick (https://ivn.us/its-official-california-voters-will-decide-on-billionaire-tax-voter-id-and-12-other-measures-this-november/) On the statewide November ballot, there are 4 high-profile propositions in which independent-minded voters will cast the most decisive votes ahead of and on Election Day: Prop 39 on Voter ID, Prop 40's billionaire tax, and two competing measures—Props. 41 and 42.
Polling shows Democrats and Republicans are sharply divided over Props. 39 and 40, while independent-minded voters are less predictable.
A UC-Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies poll (https://news.berkeley.edu/2026/08/17/california-prop-40-the-billionaire-tax-holds-lead-in-new-uc-berkeley-igs-poll/?ref=ivn.us) found 54% of likely NPP voters, specifically, opposed Prop. 39, while they were split over Prop. 40. Meanwhile, Props. 41 and 42 have large pools of undecided voters.
In a close statewide contest, a voting bloc representing nearly one-quarter of California's electorate is large enough to determine the fate of these closely watched propositions, especially when these voters do not move uniformly with either major party.
In the legislature, there are two proposed amendments — ACA 23 and ACA 24 — that will not be on the November ballot. However, they directly impact the voting rights of independent voters and their confidence in the elections process.
ACA 23 asks a fundamental question: Should the state’s top elections official run with a party label? Meanwhile, ACA 24 would explicitly make it clear that no voter can be denied the right to vote in any integral stage of the taxpayer-funded elections process for any reason.
Here is a quick guide on where all 6 proposals stand.
Proposition 39: Require Voter ID and Citizenship Verification
What It Does: Prop. 39 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/index.htm?ref=ivn.us) requires voters to show government-issued identification when casting a ballot in person. For Californians who vote by mail, they have to place the last 4 digits of their ID number on their ballot envelope.
The latter requirement is important because most voters in the state cast a mail-in ballot either by drop box, mail, or they return it to a polling location/elections office. If the number on the envelope doesn’t match their voter registration, their ballot could be invalidated.
The California Voter ID Initiative also requires election officials to produce an annual report on the percentage of voters whose citizenship has been verified and requires California to offer free voter ID cards.
Its cost, according to the Legislative Analyst Office (LAO) (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026&ref=ivn.us), falls between tens of millions and the low hundreds of millions.
IVN has followed the proposal since before it qualified for the ballot (https://ivn.us/california-voter-id-initiative-just-made-the-ballot-2026-04-27/), including how its provisions differ from the federal SAVE America Act, which has stricter citizen verification and voter ID requirements.
California’s Voter ID Initiative is Way More Chill Than Trump’s SAVE Act A proposed California ballot initiative would amend the state constitution to add an initiative that aims to “deter and detect voter fraud by maintaining accurate voter registration records and confirming eligibility to vote...” Independent Voter News Cara Brown McCormick (https://ivn.us/californias-voter-id-initiative-is-way-more-chill-than-trumps-save-act-2026-03-10/) Who Supports It: Yes on 39 is sponsored by California Asm. Carl DeMaio’s group, Reform California. Its supporters include the Transparency Foundation, Latino American Political Association, California Women's Leadership Association, and Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. The Yes campaign argues that an ID requirement would increase confidence in elections while preserving vote by mail and other existing voting options. They also emphasize the requirement for free voter ID.
Who Opposes It: The official opposition includes ACLU California Action, Common Cause and the League of Women Voters of California. US Sen. Alex Padilla, the California Nurses Association and California School Employees Association also signed arguments against the proposition. Opponents say California already verifies voters and that the measure adds unnecessary barriers and costs. They also raise privacy concerns about placing identification digits on mail-ballot envelopes and argue that voters without readily available documentation could be disproportionately affected.
Follow The Money: According to the Fair Political Practices Commission's September 8 reporting, the top contributors to the Yes campaign have put in about $15.4 million. Wisconsin businessman Richard Uihlein accounts for $10.5 million, while Reform California's ballot-measure committee has contributed just over $3 million. Nicole Shanahan, Douglas Leone, Tyler and Cameron Winklevoss and others have also contributed.
On the No side, top contributions across two committees total roughly $9.7 million. The largest listed donors include the Federated Indians of Graton Rancheria, Reed Hastings, SEIU organizations, construction labor groups, the California Teachers Association, Quinn Delaney, ACLU of Northern California, and the California Donor Table.
Note: Campaign-finance figures in this guide are based on the California Fair Political Practices Commission's top-contributor disclosures available September 8, 2026. They do not represent a complete accounting of all campaign receipts or expenditures and will change as additional reports are filed.
What Does Polling Say: In August, Berkeley IGS found 42% of likely voters supported Prop. 39 and 51% opposed. Republicans backed it 93%, while 80% of Democrats opposed it. Among NPP voters, 36% supported the measure and 54% opposed it.
CalMatters reported in March (https://www.facebook.com/calmatters/posts/a-2025-poll-from-the-uc-berkeley-institute-of-government-studies-showed-a-majori/1374297358075121/) that a 2025 Berkeley IGS poll found that 54% of voters supported showing voter ID when casting a ballot. The poll was conducted before Prop 39 was certified for the ballot.
Proposition 40: The Billionaire Tax
What It Does: Prop. 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/index.htm?ref=ivn.us) imposes a one-time tax of up to 5% on covered assets exceeding $1 billion for certain California taxpayers. Covered assets include businesses, securities, art, collectibles, and intellectual property.
Real property and some pension and retirement assets are excluded.
The LAO states that 90% of the revenue generated from this wealth tax has to be directed toward healthcare and 10% toward food assistance or education-related programs. It is projected to generate tens of billions of dollars that will be spent over several years.
LAO also says it could potentially reduce ongoing state income-tax revenue from billionaires by less than $1 billion annually.
IVN previously took a deep dive into how the wealth tax would work (https://ivn.us/how-it-really-works-the-california-billionaire-wealth-tax-2026-03-03/) and later reported on the negotiations that failed to remove it from the November ballot.
Who Supports It: Prop. 40 is sponsored by SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West. US Sen. Bernie Sanders, Rep. Ro Khanna, the California Nurses Association, and California LULAC are among those backing it, and the California Democratic Party has endorsed it.
Supporters say the tax would require an extremely small number of ultra-wealthy Californians to replace healthcare and safety-net funding affected by federal cuts. They argue that the state can raise substantial revenue from accumulated billionaire wealth without increasing taxes on middle- or lower-income Californians.
Who Opposes It: Opposition crosses some of California's usual partisan and interest-group lines. Gov. Gavin Newsom opposes it, as does Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra. Organizations that oppose it include the California Teachers Association, Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, California Medical Association, California Primary Care Association, California School Boards Association, California Professional Firefighters, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, California Chamber of Commerce, and California Taxpayers Association.
The San Francisco Democratic County Central Committee also voted 17-4 in August to oppose the measure (https://ivn.us/san-francisco-democrats-just-said-no-to-taxing-billionaires/), setting up a big-stage showdown between center-left Democrats and the DSA.
Opponents argue that taxing wealth rather than income may encourage wealthy taxpayers and businesses to leave California, reducing future income-tax collections. They also argue that a one-time revenue source does not solve California's long-term healthcare funding problems and object to exempting the new revenue from existing constitutional spending and school-funding rules.
Follow The Money: SEIU-UHW and its affiliated political committees account for about $31.4 million in top reported contributions to the committee supporting Prop. 40 and opposing Props. 41 and 42 (which are countermeasures to Prop 40).
On the other side, Building a Better California, whose top donors include Google co-founder Sergey Brin and venture capitalist John Doerr, has contributed $29.5 million to one No on 40 committee. Ripple Labs and Ripple co-founder Chris Larsen have each contributed $5 million to another opposition committee.
Altogether, the FPPC lists roughly $40.2 million in top contributions to the two Prop. 40 opposition committees.
What Does Polling Say? Berkeley IGS found 48% of likely voters supported Prop. 40 when asked in August, 41% opposed, and 11% were undecided. Democrats supported it 70%, Republicans opposed it 80%, and NPP voters were split.
One Thing Voters Need to Know About Props. 40, 41, and 42
Understanding Prop. 40 requires understanding the next two propositions.
Props. 41 and 42 contain provisions saying that conflicting measures on the same ballot do not take effect if they do not receive more Yes votes. In other words, if Prop 40 passes, but Prop. 41 or Prop. 42 also passes with more affirmative votes, a court could find the measures conflict and prevent Prop. 40 from taking effect.
Proposition 41: Ban New Taxes That Conflict with State Spending Limit (A Countermeasure to Prop. 40)
What It Does: Prop. 41 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/index.htm?ref=ivn.us) prohibits new state taxes from being designed so that their revenues are excluded from California's voter-approved state spending limit. This is important because Prop. 40 specifically exempts revenue from its billionaire tax from this limit.
Further, new statewide special taxes would require the State Auditor—an independent, nonpartisan office—to review the programs that would receive the money before voters decide on the tax and conduct recurring audits afterward.
Who Supports It: The official Yes argument (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/arguments-rebuttals.htm?ref=ivn.us) is signed by the California Society of CPAs, former California State Auditor Tom Hayes, and the California Taxpayers Association. SAN DIEGO, Calif —California voters registered No Party Preference are not a small slice of the electorate. They account for nearly 5.3 million registered voters in the state (22.82% of the electorate), and this does not count voters registered with a party that consider themselves independent-minded.
Following a record turnout in the nonpartisan Top Two primary, largely driven by independents, it is clear these voters are not only paying attention to what is happening in their state, but they are engaged, and can reshape the California political landscape.
It’s Official: California Voters Will Decide on Billionaire Tax, Voter ID, and 12 Other Measures This November Whether the billionaire wealth tax survives will come down to a simple count: if Proposition 40 beats both Proposition 41 and Proposition 42 this November, it will stand. If either of them beats it, the tax will get erased anyway. Independent Voter News Cara Brown McCormick (https://ivn.us/its-official-california-voters-will-decide-on-billionaire-tax-voter-id-and-12-other-measures-this-november/) On the statewide November ballot, there are 4 high-profile propositions in which independent-minded voters will cast the most decisive votes ahead of and on Election Day: Prop 39 on Voter ID, Prop 40's billionaire tax, and two competing measures—Props. 41 and 42.
Polling shows Democrats and Republicans are sharply divided over Props. 39 and 40, while independent-minded voters are less predictable.
A UC-Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies poll (https://news.berkeley.edu/2026/08/17/california-prop-40-the-billionaire-tax-holds-lead-in-new-uc-berkeley-igs-poll/?ref=ivn.us) found 54% of likely NPP voters, specifically, opposed Prop. 39, while they were split over Prop. 40. Meanwhile, Props. 41 and 42 have large pools of undecided voters.
In a close statewide contest, a voting bloc representing nearly one-quarter of California's electorate is large enough to determine the fate of these closely watched propositions, especially when these voters do not move uniformly with either major party.
In the legislature, there are two proposed amendments — ACA 23 and ACA 24 — that will not be on the November ballot. However, they directly impact the voting rights of independent voters and their confidence in the elections process.
ACA 23 asks a fundamental question: Should the state’s top elections official run with a party label? Meanwhile, ACA 24 would explicitly make it clear that no voter can be denied the right to vote in any integral stage of the taxpayer-funded elections process for any reason.
Here is a quick guide on where all 6 proposals stand.
Proposition 39: Require Voter ID and Citizenship Verification
What It Does: Prop. 39 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/index.htm?ref=ivn.us) requires voters to show government-issued identification when casting a ballot in person. For Californians who vote by mail, they have to place the last 4 digits of their ID number on their ballot envelope.
The latter requirement is important because most voters in the state cast a mail-in ballot either by drop box, mail, or they return it to a polling location/elections office. If the number on the envelope doesn’t match their voter registration, their ballot could be invalidated.
The California Voter ID Initiative also requires election officials to produce an annual report on the percentage of voters whose citizenship has been verified and requires California to offer free voter ID cards.
Its cost, according to the Legislative Analyst Office (LAO) (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026&ref=ivn.us), falls between tens of millions and the low hundreds of millions.
IVN has followed the proposal since before it qualified for the ballot (https://ivn.us/california-voter-id-initiative-just-made-the-ballot-2026-04-27/), including how its provisions differ from the federal SAVE America Act, which has stricter citizen verification and voter ID requirements.
California’s Voter ID Initiative is Way More Chill Than Trump’s SAVE Act A proposed California ballot initiative would amend the state constitution to add an initiative that aims to “deter and detect voter fraud by maintaining accurate voter registration records and confirming eligibility to vote...” Independent Voter News Cara Brown McCormick (https://ivn.us/californias-voter-id-initiative-is-way-more-chill-than-trumps-save-act-2026-03-10/) Who Supports It: Yes on 39 is sponsored by California Asm. Carl DeMaio’s group, Reform California. Its supporters include the Transparency Foundation, Latino American Political Association, California Women's Leadership Association, and Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. The Yes campaign argues that an ID requirement would increase confidence in elections while preserving vote by mail and other existing voting options. They also emphasize the requirement for free voter ID.
Who Opposes It: The official opposition includes ACLU California Action, Common Cause and the League of Women Voters of California. US Sen. Alex Padilla, the California Nurses Association and California School Employees Association also signed arguments against the proposition. Opponents say California already verifies voters and that the measure adds unnecessary barriers and costs. They also raise privacy concerns about placing identification digits on mail-ballot envelopes and argue that voters without readily available documentation could be disproportionately affected.
Follow The Money: According to the Fair Political Practices Commission's September 8 reporting, the top contributors to the Yes campaign have put in about $15.4 million. Wisconsin businessman Richard Uihlein accounts for $10.5 million, while Reform California's ballot-measure committee has contributed just over $3 million. Nicole Shanahan, Douglas Leone, Tyler and Cameron Winklevoss and others have also contributed.
On the No side, top contributions across two committees total roughly $9.7 million. The largest listed donors include the Federated Indians of Graton Rancheria, Reed Hastings, SEIU organizations, construction labor groups, the California Teachers Association, Quinn Delaney, ACLU of Northern California, and the California Donor Table.
Note: Campaign-finance figures in this guide are based on the California Fair Political Practices Commission's top-contributor disclosures available September 8, 2026. They do not represent a complete accounting of all campaign receipts or expenditures and will change as additional reports are filed.
What Does Polling Say: In August, Berkeley IGS found 42% of likely voters supported Prop. 39 and 51% opposed. Republicans backed it 93%, while 80% of Democrats opposed it. Among NPP voters, 36% supported the measure and 54% opposed it.
CalMatters reported in March (https://www.facebook.com/calmatters/posts/a-2025-poll-from-the-uc-berkeley-institute-of-government-studies-showed-a-majori/1374297358075121/) that a 2025 Berkeley IGS poll found that 54% of voters supported showing voter ID when casting a ballot. The poll was conducted before Prop 39 was certified for the ballot.
Proposition 40: The Billionaire Tax
What It Does: Prop. 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/index.htm?ref=ivn.us) imposes a one-time tax of up to 5% on covered assets exceeding $1 billion for certain California taxpayers. Covered assets include businesses, securities, art, collectibles, and intellectual property.
Real property and some pension and retirement assets are excluded.
The LAO states that 90% of the revenue generated from this wealth tax has to be directed toward healthcare and 10% toward food assistance or education-related programs. It is projected to generate tens of billions of dollars that will be spent over several years.
LAO also says it could potentially reduce ongoing state income-tax revenue from billionaires by less than $1 billion annually.
IVN previously took a deep dive into how the wealth tax would work (https://ivn.us/how-it-really-works-the-california-billionaire-wealth-tax-2026-03-03/) and later reported on the negotiations that failed to remove it from the November ballot.
Who Supports It: Prop. 40 is sponsored by SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West. US Sen. Bernie Sanders, Rep. Ro Khanna, the California Nurses Association, and California LULAC are among those backing it, and the California Democratic Party has endorsed it.
Supporters say the tax would require an extremely small number of ultra-wealthy Californians to replace healthcare and safety-net funding affected by federal cuts. They argue that the state can raise substantial revenue from accumulated billionaire wealth without increasing taxes on middle- or lower-income Californians.
Who Opposes It: Opposition crosses some of California's usual partisan and interest-group lines. Gov. Gavin Newsom opposes it, as does Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra. Organizations that oppose it include the California Teachers Association, Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, California Medical Association, California Primary Care Association, California School Boards Association, California Professional Firefighters, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, California Chamber of Commerce, and California Taxpayers Association.
The San Francisco Democratic County Central Committee also voted 17-4 in August to oppose the measure (https://ivn.us/san-francisco-democrats-just-said-no-to-taxing-billionaires/), setting up a big-stage showdown between center-left Democrats and the DSA.
Opponents argue that taxing wealth rather than income may encourage wealthy taxpayers and businesses to leave California, reducing future income-tax collections. They also argue that a one-time revenue source does not solve California's long-term healthcare funding problems and object to exempting the new revenue from existing constitutional spending and school-funding rules.
Follow The Money: SEIU-UHW and its affiliated political committees account for about $31.4 million in top reported contributions to the committee supporting Prop. 40 and opposing Props. 41 and 42 (which are countermeasures to Prop 40).
