SAN DIEGO, Calif —California voters registered No Party Preference are not a small slice of the electorate. They account for nearly 5.3 million registered voters in the state (22.82% of the electorate), and this does not count voters registered with a party that consider themselves independent-minded.
Following a record turnout in the nonpartisan Top Two primary, largely driven by independents, it is clear these voters are not only paying attention to what is happening in their state, but they are engaged, and can reshape the California political landscape.
It’s Official: California Voters Will Decide on Billionaire Tax, Voter ID, and 12 Other Measures This November Whether the billionaire wealth tax survives will come down to a simple count: if Proposition 40 beats both Proposition 41 and Proposition 42 this November, it will stand. If either of them beats it, the tax will get erased anyway. Independent Voter News Cara Brown McCormick (https://ivn.us/its-official-california-voters-will-decide-on-billionaire-tax-voter-id-and-12-other-measures-this-november/) On the statewide November ballot, there are 4 high-profile propositions in which independent-minded voters will cast the most decisive votes ahead of and on Election Day: Prop 39 on Voter ID, Prop 40's billionaire tax, and two competing measures—Props. 41 and 42.
Polling shows Democrats and Republicans are sharply divided over Props. 39 and 40, while independent-minded voters are less predictable.
A UC-Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies poll (https://news.berkeley.edu/2026/08/17/california-prop-40-the-billionaire-tax-holds-lead-in-new-uc-berkeley-igs-poll/?ref=ivn.us) found 54% of likely NPP voters, specifically, opposed Prop. 39, while they were split over Prop. 40. Meanwhile, Props. 41 and 42 have large pools of undecided voters.
In a close statewide contest, a voting bloc representing nearly one-quarter of California's electorate is large enough to determine the fate of these closely watched propositions, especially when these voters do not move uniformly with either major party.
In the legislature, there are two proposed amendments — ACA 23 and ACA 24 — that will not be on the November ballot. However, they directly impact the voting rights of independent voters and their confidence in the elections process.
ACA 23 asks a fundamental question: Should the state’s top elections official run with a party label? Meanwhile, ACA 24 would explicitly make it clear that no voter can be denied the right to vote in any integral stage of the taxpayer-funded elections process for any reason.
Here is a quick guide on where all 6 proposals stand.
Proposition 39: Require Voter ID and Citizenship Verification
What It Does: Prop. 39 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/index.htm?ref=ivn.us) requires voters to show government-issued identification when casting a ballot in person. For Californians who vote by mail, they have to place the last 4 digits of their ID number on their ballot envelope.
The latter requirement is important because most voters in the state cast a mail-in ballot either by drop box, mail, or they return it to a polling location/elections office. If the number on the envelope doesn’t match their voter registration, their ballot could be invalidated.
The California Voter ID Initiative also requires election officials to produce an annual report on the percentage of voters whose citizenship has been verified and requires California to offer free voter ID cards.
Its cost, according to the Legislative Analyst Office (LAO) (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026&ref=ivn.us), falls between tens of millions and the low hundreds of millions.
IVN has followed the proposal since before it qualified for the ballot (https://ivn.us/california-voter-id-initiative-just-made-the-ballot-2026-04-27/), including how its provisions differ from the federal SAVE America Act, which has stricter citizen verification and voter ID requirements.
California’s Voter ID Initiative is Way More Chill Than Trump’s SAVE Act A proposed California ballot initiative would amend the state constitution to add an initiative that aims to “deter and detect voter fraud by maintaining accurate voter registration records and confirming eligibility to vote...” Independent Voter News Cara Brown McCormick (https://ivn.us/californias-voter-id-initiative-is-way-more-chill-than-trumps-save-act-2026-03-10/) Who Supports It: Yes on 39 is sponsored by California Asm. Carl DeMaio’s group, Reform California. Its supporters include the Transparency Foundation, Latino American Political Association, California Women's Leadership Association, and Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. The Yes campaign argues that an ID requirement would increase confidence in elections while preserving vote by mail and other existing voting options. They also emphasize the requirement for free voter ID.
Who Opposes It: The official opposition includes ACLU California Action, Common Cause and the League of Women Voters of California. US Sen. Alex Padilla, the California Nurses Association and California School Employees Association also signed arguments against the proposition. Opponents say California already verifies voters and that the measure adds unnecessary barriers and costs. They also raise privacy concerns about placing identification digits on mail-ballot envelopes and argue that voters without readily available documentation could be disproportionately affected.
Follow The Money: According to the Fair Political Practices Commission's September 8 reporting, the top contributors to the Yes campaign have put in about $15.4 million. Wisconsin businessman Richard Uihlein accounts for $10.5 million, while Reform California's ballot-measure committee has contributed just over $3 million. Nicole Shanahan, Douglas Leone, Tyler and Cameron Winklevoss and others have also contributed.
On the No side, top contributions across two committees total roughly $9.7 million. The largest listed donors include the Federated Indians of Graton Rancheria, Reed Hastings, SEIU organizations, construction labor groups, the California Teachers Association, Quinn Delaney, ACLU of Northern California, and the California Donor Table.
Note: Campaign-finance figures in this guide are based on the California Fair Political Practices Commission's top-contributor disclosures available September 8, 2026. They do not represent a complete accounting of all campaign receipts or expenditures and will change as additional reports are filed.
What Does Polling Say: In August, Berkeley IGS found 42% of likely voters supported Prop. 39 and 51% opposed. Republicans backed it 93%, while 80% of Democrats opposed it. Among NPP voters, 36% supported the measure and 54% opposed it.
CalMatters reported in March (https://www.facebook.com/calmatters/posts/a-2025-poll-from-the-uc-berkeley-institute-of-government-studies-showed-a-majori/1374297358075121/) that a 2025 Berkeley IGS poll found that 54% of voters supported showing voter ID when casting a ballot. The poll was conducted before Prop 39 was certified for the ballot.
Proposition 40: The Billionaire Tax
What It Does: Prop. 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/index.htm?ref=ivn.us) imposes a one-time tax of up to 5% on covered assets exceeding $1 billion for certain California taxpayers. Covered assets include businesses, securities, art, collectibles, and intellectual property.
Real property and some pension and retirement assets are excluded.
The LAO states that 90% of the revenue generated from this wealth tax has to be directed toward healthcare and 10% toward food assistance or education-related programs. It is projected to generate tens of billions of dollars that will be spent over several years.
LAO also says it could potentially reduce ongoing state income-tax revenue from billionaires by less than $1 billion annually.
IVN previously took a deep dive into how the wealth tax would work (https://ivn.us/how-it-really-works-the-california-billionaire-wealth-tax-2026-03-03/) and later reported on the negotiations that failed to remove it from the November ballot.
Who Supports It: Prop. 40 is sponsored by SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West. US Sen. Bernie Sanders, Rep. Ro Khanna, the California Nurses Association, and California LULAC are among those backing it, and the California Democratic Party has endorsed it.
Supporters say the tax would require an extremely small number of ultra-wealthy Californians to replace healthcare and safety-net funding affected by federal cuts. They argue that the state can raise substantial revenue from accumulated billionaire wealth without increasing taxes on middle- or lower-income Californians.
Who Opposes It: Opposition crosses some of California's usual partisan and interest-group lines. Gov. Gavin Newsom opposes it, as does Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra. Organizations that oppose it include the California Teachers Association, Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, California Medical Association, California Primary Care Association, California School Boards Association, California Professional Firefighters, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, California Chamber of Commerce, and California Taxpayers Association.
The San Francisco Democratic County Central Committee also voted 17-4 in August to oppose the measure (https://ivn.us/san-francisco-democrats-just-said-no-to-taxing-billionaires/), setting up a big-stage showdown between center-left Democrats and the DSA.
Opponents argue that taxing wealth rather than income may encourage wealthy taxpayers and businesses to leave California, reducing future income-tax collections. They also argue that a one-time revenue source does not solve California's long-term healthcare funding problems and object to exempting the new revenue from existing constitutional spending and school-funding rules.
Follow The Money: SEIU-UHW and its affiliated political committees account for about $31.4 million in top reported contributions to the committee supporting Prop. 40 and opposing Props. 41 and 42 (which are countermeasures to Prop 40).
On the other side, Building a Better California, whose top donors include Google co-founder Sergey Brin and venture capitalist John Doerr, has contributed $29.5 million to one No on 40 committee. Ripple Labs and Ripple co-founder Chris Larsen have each contributed $5 million to another opposition committee.
Altogether, the FPPC lists roughly $40.2 million in top contributions to the two Prop. 40 opposition committees.
What Does Polling Say? Berkeley IGS found 48% of likely voters supported Prop. 40 when asked in August, 41% opposed, and 11% were undecided. Democrats supported it 70%, Republicans opposed it 80%, and NPP voters were split.
One Thing Voters Need to Know About Props. 40, 41, and 42
Understanding Prop. 40 requires understanding the next two propositions.
Props. 41 and 42 contain provisions saying that conflicting measures on the same ballot do not take effect if they do not receive more Yes votes. In other words, if Prop 40 passes, but Prop. 41 or Prop. 42 also passes with more affirmative votes, a court could find the measures conflict and prevent Prop. 40 from taking effect.
Proposition 41: Ban New Taxes That Conflict with State Spending Limit (A Countermeasure to Prop. 40)
What It Does: Prop. 41 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/index.htm?ref=ivn.us) prohibits new state taxes from being designed so that their revenues are excluded from California's voter-approved state spending limit. This is important because Prop. 40 specifically exempts revenue from its billionaire tax from this limit.
Further, new statewide special taxes would require the State Auditor—an independent, nonpartisan office—to review the programs that would receive the money before voters decide on the tax and conduct recurring audits afterward.
Who Supports It: The official Yes argument (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/arguments-rebuttals.htm?ref=ivn.us) is signed by the California Society of CPAs, former California State Auditor Tom Hayes, and the California Taxpayers Association. Former State Controller Steve Westly and the CalAsian Chamber of Commerce are also featured in the Yes campaign's case.
Supporters emphasize the auditing provisions. They argue voters should receive independent information about programs before approving taxes to fund them and that tax revenue should remain subject to California's existing spending restrictions.
Who Opposes It: SEIU-UHW, which sponsored Prop. 40, leads the No campaign. Opponents focus less on the merits of audits themselves and more on Prop. 41's interaction with Prop. 40. Now let me check a couple more things:
1. The research evidence on whether voter ID increases trust/confidence. Also, does the "free voter ID card" provision actually solve the access problem?
2. Any additional important consideration: the private right of action, the "citizens may seek judicial review" — litigation trap.
3. The concern about the citizenship verification and roll purges: "best efforts to verify citizenship attestations using government data" — there's no reliable national database of citizens. The DOJ's own list was found unreliable by courts (Nevada case: 185 citizens would have been disenfranchised). This creates a real risk of purging eligible citizens.
4. Check the CalBudgetCenter analysis for a fuller picture.
5. Also, is there any argument in favor that holds up? Voter impersonation fraud is essentially nonexistent in California; ID at polls wouldn't address the main fraud types (e.g., ballot harvesting/duplication). And the measure doesn't repeal signature verification, so it adds cost and delay.

Let me also check whether there's any evidence that voter ID increases turnout — the Yes argument claims states with voter ID "have seen an increase in voting." That's confounded. Peer-reviewed research: mixed but recent studies (e.g., Texas SB 1 study in Journal of Politics) found reduced turnout; other studies found minimal effect on in-person ID laws. Let me quickly check the academic literature to be balanced.

Let me also look at the LA Times last-minute guide and the CalBudgetCenter explainer, and search for research on voter ID effects on turnout.

Home (https://calbudgetcenter.org/) / Resources (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/) / Proposition 39 Explained: What Voter ID Would Mean for California
Issue Brief
Proposition 39 Explained: What Voter ID Would Mean for California
A Look at How Proposed Identification Requirements Would Impact Millions of California Voters
September 2026 | By Scott Graves (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/scott-graves/), Alissa Anderson (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/alissa-anderson/), and Leslie A. Ortiz (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/leslie-a-ortiz/)
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Proposition 39 on the November ballot would impose unnecessary, harmful, and costly new identification (ID) requirements on millions of California voters. It would harm US citizens by making it harder for them to vote, exposing them to identity theft, and putting them at risk of being erroneously removed from voter rolls. Prop. 39 is part of broader national efforts to create new barriers to voting, which primarily impact people with low incomes, young people, and people of color, limiting Californians’ say in how public tax dollars are raised and spent.
Table Of Contents
What Would Prop. 39 Do?
How Would Prop. 39 Affect Californians and the State?
Prop. 39 Is Part of a Nationwide Effort to Restrict Voting and Limit People’s Say in Policymaking
California Should Continue to Promote Voter Participation and Improve the Election Process
Prop. 39 Supporters and Opponents
What Would Prop. 39 Do?
Prop. 39 would amend California’s Constitution to add new voter ID requirements that would affect current and future voters. The measure would also impose new responsibilities on state and local officials related to election administration. Specifically, Prop. 39:
Requires Elections Officials to “Use Best Efforts” to Verify Every Registered Voter’s Citizenship Status
Current Law
Californians are required (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voting-resources/voting-california/who-can-vote-california) to be US citizens to vote. 1 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 2101(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=2101.). There are two exceptions: Oakland and San Francisco allow certain noncitizens to vote in local school board elections. To register to vote, a person must declare in writing, under penalty of perjury, that they meet all voter eligibility requirements, including that they are a US citizen (https://covr.sos.ca.gov/). 2 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 2150(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=2150.). Under federal law (https://www.justice.gov/crt/national-voter-registration-act-1993-nvra), state motor vehicle agencies — like California’s Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) — must provide residents with the opportunity to register to vote when they apply for or renew a driver’s license or state ID card and/or change their address. In California, this is known as Motor Voter (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/california-motor-voter/frequently-asked-questions). DMV customers who indicate that they are eligible to vote are registered to vote by the Secretary of State (SOS) unless they opt out. However, the DMV does not send to the SOS (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/california-motor-voter/frequently-asked-questions) information regarding customers who indicate they are not eligible to vote. Falsely claiming to be a US citizen on a voter registration application and attempting to vote would expose a person to state felony charges as well as the possibility of deportation under federal law. 3 (javascript:void(0)) For example, see California Elections Code, Section 18560(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=18560.), 8 U.S.C. Section 1227(a)(6)(a) (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title8-section1227&num=0&edition=prelim), and 18 U.S.C. Section 611 (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/611).
In addition, state law makes it a crime to:
Vote or attempt to vote more than once in an election,
Impersonate or attempt to impersonate a voter in an election, or
Apply for or cast a vote-by-mail ballot by fraudulently signing the name of a fake person, another qualified voter, or a person who is not qualified to vote. 4 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 18560(b)-(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=18560.) and Section 18578 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=18578.).
A person who is convicted of any of these crimes could be imprisoned for up to three years.
Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would require state and county election officials to “use best efforts” to verify, using “government data,” that registered voters are US citizens. The measure does not define “best efforts” or what constitutes “government data.” In addition, election officials would have to annually report the share of registered voters in each county whose citizenship status has been verified.
Requires Voters to Present Additional Identifying Information When They Cast Their Ballot
Current Law
All states, including California, already have voter ID requirements (https://electionlab.mit.edu/research/voter-identification) as required by federal law (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/hava-id-standards). For example, to register to vote, Californians must provide (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration) a California driver’s license or state ID number or the last four digits of their Social Security Number (SSN) if they lack a driver’s license or ID card. Californians who lack a driver’s license, a state ID card, or a SSN are assigned a unique identifier (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration) to validate their registration. Californians generally are not required (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration) to present an ID when voting. 5 (javascript:void(0)) Californians may need to show (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration) an acceptable form of ID when they vote by mail or in person if all of the following apply: 1) they’re voting for the first time in a federal election, 2) they registered by mail or online, and 3) they did not provide a California ID or SSN when registering. Acceptable forms of ID (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/hava-id-standards) include, but aren’t limited to, a California driver’s license or state ID card, a US passport, a student or military ID, a utility bill, and a bank statement.
When voting by mail, California voters sign the outside of their ballot envelope, and elections officials verify the signature before counting the ballot. 6 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 3011(a)(7) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=3011.) and Section 3019 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=3019.). Voters must be given an opportunity to correct or “cure” their ballot if they failed to sign the envelope or if their signature does not match the signature on file. 7 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Sections 3019(c)-(e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=3019.).
When voting in person, California voters state their name and address and sign a list of registered voters under penalty of perjury. 8 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 14216(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=14216.). While election officials do not verify (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm) the signatures of in-person voters before counting their ballots, counties have procedures in place to prevent voter fraud. 9 (javascript:void(0)) For example, in many counties, poll workers are able to look up voting records in real time to ensure that a voter has not already cast a ballot in the election. This applies to counties that participate (https://www.sos.ca.gov/voters-choice-act/vca-participating-counties) in California’s Voter’s Choice Act (https://www.sos.ca.gov/voters-choice-act) as well as to counties that have adopted the Sign, Scan, and Go (https://www.placercountyelections.gov/sign-scan-go/) option. As noted above, it is a crime in California to fraudulently vote in an election, to vote more than once, or to impersonate another voter. Penalties range from up to one year in a county jail to up to three years in state prison.
Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would impose new requirements on Californians to cast a ballot in person or mail a ballot.
To vote in person:
Voters would have to present a “government-issued” ID when they arrive at their polling place. Prop. 39 does not specifically define what “government-issued” ID means, so the Legislature would need to clarify which types of ID a voter could present to prove their identity. 10 (javascript:void(0)) Prop. 39 says broadly that “government-issued” ID “means documentation that allows conclusive verification of the voter’s identity.”
To vote by mail:
All new and existing voters would have to select a “government-issued” ID that would be reflected in their “voter registration record.” This requirement effectively means that people who are currently registered to vote would have to re-register to provide their chosen ID to election officials.
When voting, voters would have to write on the outside of their ballot envelope the last four digits of a “unique identifying number” from the “government-issued” ID that they selected for the purpose of voting. 11 (javascript:void(0)) The government-issued ID that voters choose for this purpose would have to subsequently be made available to them “on request by phone or electronically.”
Election officials would verify that the four digits written on the envelope match the last four digits of the ID number in the voter’s registration record.
Requires the State to Create a New Voter ID Card
Current Law
California currently allows Californians to apply for three types of ID cards (https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/driver-licenses-identification-cards/identification-id-cards/) in addition to drivers’ licenses that are used to prove identity or age. 12 (javascript:void(0)) The ID cards are issued by the California Department of Motor Vehicles as alternatives to a driver’s license and cannot be used to operate a motor vehicle.
Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would require the state to provide a voter ID card to eligible voters who request one. Voters could use this optional ID as their “government-issued” ID for voting by mail or in person. This card would be provided to voters free of charge.
Requires Ongoing State Audits of How the State and Counties Are Complying with Prop. 39
Current Law
California’s independently elected (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/california-state-constitutional-offices-defined/) Secretary of State oversees (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/about-agency) all elections in the state, including ensuring election laws are enforced, testing and approving voting equipment, compiling election returns, and certifying election results.
In addition, California’s independent, nonpartisan State Auditor (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/about-us/) conducts performance audits and investigations of various state and local government agencies and recommends solutions for improving services. However, the State Auditor currently does not have a formal, ongoing role in auditing California’s elections or evaluating election administration.
Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would require the State Auditor, in odd-numbered years, to audit state and county compliance with Prop. 39 and report any recommendations for improvement.
Requires the State Legislature to Pass Laws to Implement Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would require the Legislature to “promptly enact laws” to implement the measure. For example, legislators would have to define which kinds of “government-issued” ID would be acceptable for voting as well as clarify what it means to make a “best effort” to verify a voter’s citizenship status. Prop. 39 would also require the Legislature to establish rules for military and overseas voters that are consistent with federal law.
Allows Citizens to Sue the State or Any County for Not Complying with Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would allow private citizens to sue the state and/or any county for any alleged noncompliance with the initiative. The measure does not specify what kind of evidence would be required to file a lawsuit.
How Would Prop. 39 Affect Californians and the State?
Prop. 39 Would Waste Resources By Addressing a Nonexistent Problem
The voter ID requirements that Prop. 39 would establish provide a “solution” to a nonexistent problem. This measure is based on the false premise that voter fraud — casting a ballot when one is not eligible to vote — is undermining election integrity. However, research shows that voter fraud is exceedingly rare. For example:
Using a comprehensive database tracking election fraud (https://www.brookings.edu/articles/how-widespread-is-election-fraud-in-the-united-states-not-very/) that was created by the right-wing think tank Heritage Foundation, the Brookings Institute found across more than 200 federal elections held in recent decades, the share of fraudulent votes cast were infinitesimally small — ranging from roughly 3 to 15 votes out of 10 million in seven states with close election outcomes. The study concluded that “isolated instances of fraud do not constitute a widespread trend” and that “no election outcome in the US has ever been altered by ballot fraud.”
Summarizing findings across numerous academic studies and investigative reports, the Brennan Center for Justice (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/debunking-voter-fraud-myth) concludes that cases of voter impersonation fraud are extremely rare and do not happen “on a scale even close to that necessary to ‘rig’ an election.” For instance, their seminal report, The Truth About Voter Fraud (https://www.brennancenter.org/media/179/download/Report_Truth-About-Voter-Fraud.pdf?inline=1), concluded that “it is more likely that an individual will be struck by lightning than that [they] will impersonate another voter at the polls.”
Voter fraud among noncitizens is also extremely rare. The Brennan Center (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/noncitizen-voting-vanishingly-rare) synthesized findings from comprehensive studies, state investigations, and nationwide surveys across more than two decades and concluded that “actual incidents of noncitizens voting is not a significant occurrence.” For instance:
One national survey (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/noncitizen-voting-missing-millions) of 44 election administrators representing 42 jurisdictions in 12 states, including officials in eight of the 10 jurisdictions with the largest populations of noncitizens nationally, found that in the 2016 election, officials referred only about 30 incidents of suspected noncitizen voting for further investigation or prosecution — amounting to 0.0001% of votes cast.
The Bipartisan Policy Institute (https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/four-things-to-know-about-noncitizen-voting/) concluded that “there is no evidence that noncitizen voting has ever been significant enough to impact an election’s outcome.” Allegations of noncitizens voting often come out of voter registration audits, but further investigation into these claims often shows that individuals were flagged as noncitizens erroneously.
The libertarian think tank Cato Institute (https://www.cato.org/blog/noncitizens-dont-illegally-vote-detectable-numbers) found that “there is no good evidence that noncitizens voted illegally [in the 2020 election] in large enough numbers to actually shift the outcome of elections or even change the number of electoral votes.”
Additionally, while proponents of Prop. 39 argue that imposing additional ID requirements will strengthen voters’ trust in California’s election process, evidence for this claim is lacking. One study (https://review.law.stanford.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2016/08/6_-_Persily_-_Stan._L._Rev.pdf) found that registered voters had roughly equal confidence that votes were counted accurately whether they were in states with strict voter ID laws or states with the minimum ID requirements mandated by federal law.
Subsequent studies by researchers at the University of California Riverside and Western Washington University looking at voter perceptions in 2014 (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/1532440015624102?) and following the 2020 US presidential election (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/10659129231206179) found that strict voter ID laws and the quality of election administration more generally had little to no effect on voter confidence. ## Abstract
Widespread concern that voter identification laws suppress turnout among racial and ethnic minorities has made empirical evaluations of these laws crucial.
But problems with administrative records and survey data impede such evaluations.
We replicate and extend Hajnal, Lajevardi, and Nielson’s 2017 article, which concludes that voter ID laws decrease turnout among minorities, using validated turnout data from five national surveys conducted between 2006 and 2014.
We show that the results of their article are a product of data inaccuracies, the presented evidence does not support the stated conclusion, and alternative model specifications produce highly variable results.
When errors are corrected, one can recover positive, negative, or null estimates of the effect of voter ID laws on turnout, precluding firm conclusions.
We highlight more general problems with available data for research on election administration, and we identify more appropriate data sources for research on state voting laws’ effects.

Proposition 39 Explained: What Voter ID Would Mean for California
A Look at How Proposed Identification Requirements Would Impact Millions of California Voters
September 2026 | By Scott Graves (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/scott-graves/), Alissa Anderson (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/alissa-anderson/), and Leslie A. Ortiz (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/leslie-a-ortiz/)
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Proposition 39 on the November ballot would impose unnecessary, harmful, and costly new identification (ID) requirements on millions of California voters. It would harm US citizens by making it harder for them to vote, exposing them to identity theft, and putting them at risk of being erroneously removed from voter rolls. Prop. 39 is part of broader national efforts to create new barriers to voting, which primarily impact people with low incomes, young people, and people of color, limiting Californians’ say in how public tax dollars are raised and spent.

Prop. 39 Supporters and Opponents
What Would Prop. 39 Do?
Prop. 39 would amend California’s Constitution to add new voter ID requirements that would affect current and future voters. The measure would also impose new responsibilities on state and local officials related to election administration. Specifically, Prop. 39:
Requires Elections Officials to “Use Best Efforts” to Verify Every Registered Voter’s Citizenship Status
Current Law

Proposition 39 Explained: What Voter ID Would Mean for California
A Look at How Proposed Identification Requirements Would Impact Millions of California Voters
September 2026 | By Scott Graves (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/scott-graves/), Alissa Anderson (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/alissa-anderson/), and Leslie A. Ortiz (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/leslie-a-ortiz/)
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Proposition 39 on the November ballot would impose unnecessary, harmful, and costly new identification (ID) requirements on millions of California voters. It would harm US citizens by making it harder for them to vote, exposing them to identity theft, and putting them at risk of being erroneously removed from voter rolls. Prop. 39 is part of broader national efforts to create new barriers to voting, which primarily impact people with low incomes, young people, and people of color, limiting Californians’ say in how public tax dollars are raised and spent.

The study concluded that “isolated instances of fraud do not constitute a widespread trend” and that “no election outcome in the US has ever been altered by ballot fraud.”
Summarizing findings across numerous academic studies and investigative reports, the Brennan Center for Justice (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/debunking-voter-fraud-myth) concludes that cases of voter impersonation fraud are extremely rare and do not happen “on a scale even close to that necessary to ‘rig’ an election.” For instance, their seminal report, The Truth About Voter Fraud (https://www.brennancenter.org/media/179/download/Report_Truth-About-Voter-Fraud.pdf?inline=1), concluded that “it is more likely that an individual will be struck by lightning than that [they] will impersonate another voter at the polls.”
Voter fraud among noncitizens is also extremely rare. The Brennan Center (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/noncitizen-voting-vanishingly-rare) synthesized findings from comprehensive studies, state investigations, and nationwide surveys across more than two decades and concluded that “actual incidents of noncitizens voting is not a significant occurrence.” For instance:
One national survey (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/noncitizen-voting-missing-millions) of 44 election administrators representing 42 jurisdictions in 12 states, including officials in eight of the 10 jurisdictions with the largest populations of noncitizens nationally, found that in the 2016 election, officials referred only about 30 incidents of suspected noncitizen voting for further investigation or prosecution — amounting to 0.0001% of votes cast.
The Bipartisan Policy Institute (https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/four-things-to-know-about-noncitizen-voting/) concluded that “there is no evidence that noncitizen voting has ever been significant enough to impact an election’s outcome.” Allegations of noncitizens voting often come out of voter registration audits, but further investigation into these claims often shows that individuals were flagged as noncitizens erroneously.
The libertarian think tank Cato Institute (https://www.cato.org/blog/noncitizens-dont-illegally-vote-detectable-numbers) found that “there is no good evidence that noncitizens voted illegally [in the 2020 election] in large enough numbers to actually shift the outcome of elections or even change the number of electoral votes.”

## Abstract
Widespread concern that voter identification laws suppress turnout among racial and ethnic minorities has made empirical evaluations of these laws crucial.
But problems with administrative records and survey data impede such evaluations.
We replicate and extend Hajnal, Lajevardi, and Nielson’s 2017 article, which concludes that voter ID laws decrease turnout among minorities, using validated turnout data from five national surveys conducted between 2006 and 2014.
We show that the results of their article are a product of data inaccuracies, the presented evidence does not support the stated conclusion, and alternative model specifications produce highly variable results.
When errors are corrected, one can recover positive, negative, or null estimates of the effect of voter ID laws on turnout, precluding firm conclusions.
We highlight more general problems with available data for research on election administration, and we identify more appropriate data sources for research on state voting laws’ effects.

IVN's guide is neutral-ish (describes both sides) but notes that 54% of NPP voters opposed Prop 39 in the Berkeley poll. IVN doesn't appear to endorse.

Now let me check a couple more things:
1. The research evidence on whether voter ID increases trust/confidence. Also, does the "free voter ID card" provision actually solve the access problem?
2. Any additional important consideration: the private right of action, the "citizens may seek judicial review" — litigation trap.
3. The concern about the citizenship verification and roll purges: "best efforts to verify citizenship attestations using government data" — there's no reliable national database of citizens. Issue Brief
Proposition 39 Explained: What Voter ID Would Mean for California
A Look at How Proposed Identification Requirements Would Impact Millions of California Voters
September 2026 | By Scott Graves (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/scott-graves/), Alissa Anderson (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/alissa-anderson/), and Leslie A. Ortiz (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/leslie-a-ortiz/)
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Proposition 39 on the November ballot would impose unnecessary, harmful, and costly new identification (ID) requirements on millions of California voters. It would harm US citizens by making it harder for them to vote, exposing them to identity theft, and putting them at risk of being erroneously removed from voter rolls. Prop. 39 is part of broader national efforts to create new barriers to voting, which primarily impact people with low incomes, young people, and people of color, limiting Californians’ say in how public tax dollars are raised and spent.
Table Of Contents
What Would Prop. 39 Do?
How Would Prop. 39 Affect Californians and the State?
Prop. 39 Is Part of a Nationwide Effort to Restrict Voting and Limit People’s Say in Policymaking
California Should Continue to Promote Voter Participation and Improve the Election Process
Prop. 39 Supporters and Opponents
What Would Prop. 39 Do?
Prop. 39 would amend California’s Constitution to add new voter ID requirements that would affect current and future voters. The measure would also impose new responsibilities on state and local officials related to election administration. Specifically, Prop. 39:
Requires Elections Officials to “Use Best Efforts” to Verify Every Registered Voter’s Citizenship Status
Current Law
Californians are required (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voting-resources/voting-california/who-can-vote-california) to be US citizens to vote. 1 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 2101(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=2101.). There are two exceptions: Oakland and San Francisco allow certain noncitizens to vote in local school board elections. To register to vote, a person must declare in writing, under penalty of perjury, that they meet all voter eligibility requirements, including that they are a US citizen (https://covr.sos.ca.gov/). 2 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 2150(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=2150.). Under federal law (https://www.justice.gov/crt/national-voter-registration-act-1993-nvra), state motor vehicle agencies — like California’s Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) — must provide residents with the opportunity to register to vote when they apply for or renew a driver’s license or state ID card and/or change their address. In California, this is known as Motor Voter (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/california-motor-voter/frequently-asked-questions). DMV customers who indicate that they are eligible to vote are registered to vote by the Secretary of State (SOS) unless they opt out. However, the DMV does not send to the SOS (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/california-motor-voter/frequently-asked-questions) information regarding customers who indicate they are not eligible to vote. Falsely claiming to be a US citizen on a voter registration application and attempting to vote would expose a person to state felony charges as well as the possibility of deportation under federal law. 3 (javascript:void(0)) For example, see California Elections Code, Section 18560(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=18560.), 8 U.S.C. Section 1227(a)(6)(a) (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title8-section1227&num=0&edition=prelim), and 18 U.S.C. Section 611 (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/611).
In addition, state law makes it a crime to:
Vote or attempt to vote more than once in an election,
Impersonate or attempt to impersonate a voter in an election, or
Apply for or cast a vote-by-mail ballot by fraudulently signing the name of a fake person, another qualified voter, or a person who is not qualified to vote. 4 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 18560(b)-(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=18560.) and Section 18578 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=18578.).
A person who is convicted of any of these crimes could be imprisoned for up to three years.
Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would require state and county election officials to “use best efforts” to verify, using “government data,” that registered voters are US citizens. The measure does not define “best efforts” or what constitutes “government data.” In addition, election officials would have to annually report the share of registered voters in each county whose citizenship status has been verified.
Requires Voters to Present Additional Identifying Information When They Cast Their Ballot
Current Law
All states, including California, already have voter ID requirements (https://electionlab.mit.edu/research/voter-identification) as required by federal law (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/hava-id-standards). For example, to register to vote, Californians must provide (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration) a California driver’s license or state ID number or the last four digits of their Social Security Number (SSN) if they lack a driver’s license or ID card. Californians who lack a driver’s license, a state ID card, or a SSN are assigned a unique identifier (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration) to validate their registration. Californians generally are not required (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration) to present an ID when voting. 5 (javascript:void(0)) Californians may need to show (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration) an acceptable form of ID when they vote by mail or in person if all of the following apply: 1) they’re voting for the first time in a federal election, 2) they registered by mail or online, and 3) they did not provide a California ID or SSN when registering. Acceptable forms of ID (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/hava-id-standards) include, but aren’t limited to, a California driver’s license or state ID card, a US passport, a student or military ID, a utility bill, and a bank statement.
When voting by mail, California voters sign the outside of their ballot envelope, and elections officials verify the signature before counting the ballot. 6 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 3011(a)(7) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=3011.) and Section 3019 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=3019.). Voters must be given an opportunity to correct or “cure” their ballot if they failed to sign the envelope or if their signature does not match the signature on file. 7 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Sections 3019(c)-(e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=3019.).
When voting in person, California voters state their name and address and sign a list of registered voters under penalty of perjury. 8 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 14216(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=14216.). While election officials do not verify (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm) the signatures of in-person voters before counting their ballots, counties have procedures in place to prevent voter fraud. 9 (javascript:void(0)) For example, in many counties, poll workers are able to look up voting records in real time to ensure that a voter has not already cast a ballot in the election. This applies to counties that participate (https://www.sos.ca.gov/voters-choice-act/vca-participating-counties) in California’s Voter’s Choice Act (https://www.sos.ca.gov/voters-choice-act) as well as to counties that have adopted the Sign, Scan, and Go (https://www.placercountyelections.gov/sign-scan-go/) option. As noted above, it is a crime in California to fraudulently vote in an election, to vote more than once, or to impersonate another voter. Penalties range from up to one year in a county jail to up to three years in state prison.
Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would impose new requirements on Californians to cast a ballot in person or mail a ballot.
To vote in person:
Voters would have to present a “government-issued” ID when they arrive at their polling place. Prop. 39 does not specifically define what “government-issued” ID means, so the Legislature would need to clarify which types of ID a voter could present to prove their identity. 10 (javascript:void(0)) Prop. 39 says broadly that “government-issued” ID “means documentation that allows conclusive verification of the voter’s identity.”
To vote by mail:
All new and existing voters would have to select a “government-issued” ID that would be reflected in their “voter registration record.” This requirement effectively means that people who are currently registered to vote would have to re-register to provide their chosen ID to election officials.
When voting, voters would have to write on the outside of their ballot envelope the last four digits of a “unique identifying number” from the “government-issued” ID that they selected for the purpose of voting. 11 (javascript:void(0)) The government-issued ID that voters choose for this purpose would have to subsequently be made available to them “on request by phone or electronically.”
Election officials would verify that the four digits written on the envelope match the last four digits of the ID number in the voter’s registration record.
Requires the State to Create a New Voter ID Card
Current Law
California currently allows Californians to apply for three types of ID cards (https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/driver-licenses-identification-cards/identification-id-cards/) in addition to drivers’ licenses that are used to prove identity or age. 12 (javascript:void(0)) The ID cards are issued by the California Department of Motor Vehicles as alternatives to a driver’s license and cannot be used to operate a motor vehicle.
Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would require the state to provide a voter ID card to eligible voters who request one. Voters could use this optional ID as their “government-issued” ID for voting by mail or in person. This card would be provided to voters free of charge.
Requires Ongoing State Audits of How the State and Counties Are Complying with Prop. 39
Current Law
California’s independently elected (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/california-state-constitutional-offices-defined/) Secretary of State oversees (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/about-agency) all elections in the state, including ensuring election laws are enforced, testing and approving voting equipment, compiling election returns, and certifying election results.
In addition, California’s independent, nonpartisan State Auditor (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/about-us/) conducts performance audits and investigations of various state and local government agencies and recommends solutions for improving services. However, the State Auditor currently does not have a formal, ongoing role in auditing California’s elections or evaluating election administration.
Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would require the State Auditor, in odd-numbered years, to audit state and county compliance with Prop. 39 and report any recommendations for improvement.
Requires the State Legislature to Pass Laws to Implement Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would require the Legislature to “promptly enact laws” to implement the measure. For example, legislators would have to define which kinds of “government-issued” ID would be acceptable for voting as well as clarify what it means to make a “best effort” to verify a voter’s citizenship status. Prop. 39 would also require the Legislature to establish rules for military and overseas voters that are consistent with federal law.
Allows Citizens to Sue the State or Any County for Not Complying with Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would allow private citizens to sue the state and/or any county for any alleged noncompliance with the initiative. The measure does not specify what kind of evidence would be required to file a lawsuit.
How Would Prop. 39 Affect Californians and the State?
Prop. 39 Would Waste Resources By Addressing a Nonexistent Problem
The voter ID requirements that Prop. 39 would establish provide a “solution” to a nonexistent problem. This measure is based on the false premise that voter fraud — casting a ballot when one is not eligible to vote — is undermining election integrity. However, research shows that voter fraud is exceedingly rare. For example:
Using a comprehensive database tracking election fraud (https://www.brookings.edu/articles/how-widespread-is-election-fraud-in-the-united-states-not-very/) that was created by the right-wing think tank Heritage Foundation, the Brookings Institute found across more than 200 federal elections held in recent decades, the share of fraudulent votes cast were infinitesimally small — ranging from roughly 3 to 15 votes out of 10 million in seven states with close election outcomes. The study concluded that “isolated instances of fraud do not constitute a widespread trend” and that “no election outcome in the US has ever been altered by ballot fraud.”
Summarizing findings across numerous academic studies and investigative reports, the Brennan Center for Justice (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/debunking-voter-fraud-myth) concludes that cases of voter impersonation fraud are extremely rare and do not happen “on a scale even close to that necessary to ‘rig’ an election.” For instance, their seminal report, The Truth About Voter Fraud (https://www.brennancenter.org/media/179/download/Report_Truth-About-Voter-Fraud.pdf?inline=1), concluded that “it is more likely that an individual will be struck by lightning than that [they] will impersonate another voter at the polls.”
Voter fraud among noncitizens is also extremely rare. The Brennan Center (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/noncitizen-voting-vanishingly-rare) synthesized findings from comprehensive studies, state investigations, and nationwide surveys across more than two decades and concluded that “actual incidents of noncitizens voting is not a significant occurrence.” For instance:
One national survey (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/noncitizen-voting-missing-millions) of 44 election administrators representing 42 jurisdictions in 12 states, including officials in eight of the 10 jurisdictions with the largest populations of noncitizens nationally, found that in the 2016 election, officials referred only about 30 incidents of suspected noncitizen voting for further investigation or prosecution — amounting to 0.0001% of votes cast.
The Bipartisan Policy Institute (https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/four-things-to-know-about-noncitizen-voting/) concluded that “there is no evidence that noncitizen voting has ever been significant enough to impact an election’s outcome.” Allegations of noncitizens voting often come out of voter registration audits, but further investigation into these claims often shows that individuals were flagged as noncitizens erroneously.
The libertarian think tank Cato Institute (https://www.cato.org/blog/noncitizens-dont-illegally-vote-detectable-numbers) found that “there is no good evidence that noncitizens voted illegally [in the 2020 election] in large enough numbers to actually shift the outcome of elections or even change the number of electoral votes.”
Additionally, while proponents of Prop. 39 argue that imposing additional ID requirements will strengthen voters’ trust in California’s election process, evidence for this claim is lacking. One study (https://review.law.stanford.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2016/08/6_-_Persily_-_Stan._L._Rev.pdf) found that registered voters had roughly equal confidence that votes were counted accurately whether they were in states with strict voter ID laws or states with the minimum ID requirements mandated by federal law.
Subsequent studies by researchers at the University of California Riverside and Western Washington University looking at voter perceptions in 2014 (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/1532440015624102?) and following the 2020 US presidential election (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/10659129231206179) found that strict voter ID laws and the quality of election administration more generally had little to no effect on voter confidence. This and other research (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/10659129241283169) suggests this may be because voters view election laws through a partisan lens and their confidence may be more heavily influenced by partisan rhetoric and whether their preferred candidate wins or loses an election. 13 (javascript:void(0)) See Lonna Rae Atkeson, Eli McKown-Dawson, and Robert M. Stein, “The Costs of Voting and Voter Confidence,” Political Research Quarter

Good balance. The academic literature on in-person photo ID laws is genuinely mixed: the strongest recent study (Cantoni & Pons, QJE 2021) found no negative effect on turnout from strict in-person ID laws, and also found "no effect on fraud — actual or perceived" (i.e., strict ID laws do not increase perceived confidence either). Meanwhile, mail-ballot ID-number-matching requirements (Texas SB 1) demonstrably caused large spikes in ballot rejections and reduced participation among those affected.

That's an important distinction: Prop 39's biggest operational risk is not the in-person ID requirement (which research suggests has modest effects), but the mail-ballot four-digit matching requirement with NO cure process — applied to ~13 million mail ballots in a state where 80%+ vote by mail. Texas showed this exact mechanism produced a 12% rejection rate initially, with ~90% of affected voters not finding another way to vote.

Let me also check:
1. Cantoni & Pons finding on "perceived fraud" — that's important for the "trust" argument. Let me verify.
2. Whether Prop 39 conflicts with the state constitution's free elections clause or the NVRA — legal challenges likely after passage.
3. Any additional consideration on the "citizenship verification" component — the risk of erroneously purging naturalized citizens. There's no reliable federal database. DHS data has proven unreliable (Nevada: 185 citizens would have been disenfranchised).
4. Also the private right of action — "Citizens may seek judicial review and remedy of the State's or any county's compliance" — litigation trap.
5. Let's also check the LA Times last-minute guide position and whether there's a moderate case for yes. And check GrowSF/other YIMBY groups.

Let me also double-check the claim in the Yes argument that signature mismatch rejected 100,000+ ballots — verified false per official records (71,387 statewide Nov 2024).

Also check: does Prop 39 create a problem for voters with no driver's license/SSN? They'd get a unique identifier assigned at registration — but Prop 39 requires designating a "government-issued identification" number. Those without any government ID would need the free voter ID card.

One more thing to check: whether there's an argument that the free voter ID card mitigates. And the LAO estimate of costs.

Let me do a couple more searches: Cantoni & Pons perceived fraud; and any analysis of Prop 39's effect on the 2028 election / potential federal preemption challenge (materiality provision).

content.thinking:
Good balance. The academic literature on in-person photo ID laws is genuinely mixed: the strongest recent study (Cantoni & Pons, QJE 2021) found no negative effect on turnout from strict in-person ID laws, and also found "no effect on fraud — actual or perceived" (i.e., strict ID laws do not increase perceived confidence either). Meanwhile, mail-ballot ID-number-matching requirements (Texas SB 1) demonstrably caused large spikes in ballot rejections and reduced participation among those affected.

That's an important distinction: Prop 39's biggest operational risk is not the in-person ID requirement (which research suggests has modest effects), but the mail-ballot four-digit matching requirement with NO cure process — applied to ~13 million mail ballots in a state where 80%+ vote by mail. Texas showed this exact mechanism produced a 12% rejection rate initially, with ~90% of affected voters not finding another way to vote.

Let me also check:
1. Cantoni & Pons finding on "perceived fraud" — that's important for the "trust" argument. Let me verify.
2. Whether Prop 39 conflicts with the state constitution's free elections clause or the NVRA — legal challenges likely after passage.
3. Any additional consideration on the "citizenship verification" component — the risk of erroneously purging naturalized citizens. There's no reliable federal database. DHS data has proven unreliable (Nevada: 185 citizens would have been disenfranchised).
4. Also the private right of action — "Citizens may seek judicial review and remedy of the State's or any county's compliance" — litigation trap.
5. Let's also check the LA Times last-minute guide position and whether there's a moderate case for yes. And check GrowSF/other YIMBY groups.

Let me also double-check the claim in the Yes argument that signature mismatch rejected 100,000+ ballots — verified false per official records (71,387 statewide Nov 2024).

Also check: does Prop 39 create a problem for voters with no driver's license/SSN? They'd get a unique identifier assigned at registration — but Prop 39 requires designating a "government-issued identification" number. Those without any government ID would need the free voter ID card.

One more thing to check: whether there's an argument that the free voter ID card mitigates. And the LAO estimate of costs.

Let me do a couple more searches: Cantoni & Pons perceived fraud; and any analysis of Prop 39's effect on the 2028 election / potential federal preemption challenge (materiality provision).

I now have a very comprehensive picture. Let me do a final couple of checks:

1. The Arizona/Mi Familia Vota case shows that ID-number matching requirements on mail ballots have been held to violate the federal Materiality Provision. That's a serious legal risk for Prop 39 — a constitutional amendment that could be struck down or enjoined in part.

2. Let me verify one more thing: the "trust" claim. Cantoni & Pons found strict ID laws had NO effect on perceived fraud or belief that elections were fair. That directly undercuts the Yes campaign's central argument.

3. Let me also double-check whether there's a strong case FOR. Points in favor:
   - Public opinion: voter ID is popular in the abstract; many Californians support it in principle (2025 Berkeley poll: 54% supported showing voter ID).
   - In-person ID requirement is modest and research suggests minimal turnout effects (Cantoni & Pons).
   - Free voter ID card is guaranteed.
   - Citizenship verification and roll maintenance and audits are, in isolation, reasonable — and counties have asked for authority to join multistate roll-maintenance organizations (ERIC successors).
   - Bipartisan framing; some Democrats/Independents signed the petition.
   - Would harmonize California with the majority of states that require ID.

   Points against (stronger in my assessment):
   - The measure is poorly drafted: it doesn't define acceptable IDs, doesn't define "best efforts" or "government data," leaves key details to a Legislature that must act "promptly" — yet is "self-executing," meaning it takes effect immediately upon certification without implementing rules. That's a recipe for chaos and litigation in the first election it applies to.
   - No notice-and-cure provision for mail ballots with wrong/missing digits — while California's current signature-mismatch system has a robust 22-day cure. Texas's near-identical mail-ballot ID-matching rule produced a 12.38% rejection rate in the first election (up from ~1%), with ~82-90% of those rejections attributable to the ID requirement, and a peer-reviewed Journal of Politics study found ~90% of affected voters didn't find another way to participate. In California, 80%+ of ballots are cast by mail — so this is the highest-risk provision.
   - The measure does NOT repeal signature verification — so it adds a second layer rather than replacing one, contradicting the Yes campaign's implied "faster/easier" claim (a judge found such claims false and misleading).
   - Yes campaign's central factual claim (100,000+ ballots rejected for signature mismatch) is not supported by official records (71,387 statewide in Nov 2024).
   - A judge found the Yes campaign's claims that it makes voting easier, saves money, and contains privacy protections to be false and misleading; supporters dropped them.
   - Costs: LAO estimates tens of millions to low hundreds of millions per year, ongoing.
   - It solves a nonexistent problem: no evidence of systemic fraud (14-county grand jury review via State Library; Heritage Foundation database shows 71 CA cases 1982–2025). Even the DOJ's own 20,000-name noncitizen list was found unreliable by federal courts (Nevada: 185 citizens would have been disenfranchised).
   - It wouldn't deliver its promised benefit: Cantoni & Pons (QJE) found strict ID laws have no effect on actual OR perceived fraud, and no effect on beliefs that elections were fair. UC Riverside/Western Washington studies similarly found little to no effect on voter confidence. So the "trust" rationale is empirically unsupported.
   - Privacy: requires writing partial SSN/driver's license digits on the outside of a ballot envelope, which passes through mail handling, drop boxes, and is visible to anyone who handles it — an identity-theft exposure with no compensating benefit.
   - Litigation trap: private right of action for "citizens" to sue the state or any county over compliance, with undefined standards, in a state already known for CEQA-style abuse. Election law expert Justin Levitt called it a "generic litigation trap." Plus high risk of federal Materiality Provision / NVRA challenges (as in Arizona's Mi Familia Vota).
   - Disparate impact: ~2.7 million Californians (11% of eligible voters) lack a driver's license; 13% have expired/outdated ones; disproportionately people of color, young, disabled, low-income. Married women who changed names face extra hurdles.
   - The citizenship-verification mandate has no workable data source (no comprehensive federal citizen database), risks erroneously flagging naturalized citizens, and would generate annual public "verification percentage" reports that could be weaponized politically.
   - It would write this into the state Constitution, where it's very hard to fix later (requires another statewide vote) — a poorly drafted, undefined standard locked into the constitution is bad governance regardless of one's view on voter ID.
   - Funding: $36.5M, two-thirds from out-of-state billionaire Richard Uihlein ($17M) plus Airbnb co-founder/White House official Joe Gebbia ($8M) — CalMatters reports national GOP donors view it as a test case for other swing states, not a California-specific reform.
   - Nearly every major California newspaper editorial board that examined it recommended NO (Sacramento Bee/McClatchy CA boards, SF Chronicle, LA Times, San Diego Union-Tribune, Mercury News/East Bay Times, Daily Californian). The Secretary of State, county registrars, and election administrators oppose it. Only a few (Pasadena Star-News) endorsed yes.
   - Polling: trailing consistently — PPIC Oct: 41% yes / 58% no; Berkeley IGS Sept: 39/52; Citrin-POLITICO Oct: 42/51. Even no-party-preference voters oppose by 13+ points.

Verdict: NO.

   - Yes campaign's central factual claim (100,000+ ballots rejected for signature mismatch) is not supported by official records (71,387 statewide in Nov 2024).
   - A judge found the Yes campaign's claims that it makes voting easier, saves money, and contains privacy protections to be false and misleading; supporters dropped them.
   - Costs: LAO estimates tens of millions to low hundreds of millions per year, ongoing.
   - It solves a nonexistent problem: no evidence of systemic fraud (14-county grand jury review via State Library; Heritage Foundation database shows 71 CA cases 1982–2025). Even the DOJ's own 20,000-name noncitizen list was found unreliable by federal courts (Nevada: 185 citizens would have been disenfranchised).
   - It wouldn't deliver its promised benefit: Cantoni & Pons (QJE) found strict ID laws have no effect on actual OR perceived fraud, and no effect on beliefs that elections were fair. UC Riverside/Western Washington studies similarly found little to no effect on voter confidence. So the "trust" rationale is empirically unsupported.
   - Privacy: requires writing partial SSN/driver's license digits on the outside of a ballot envelope, which passes through mail handling, drop boxes, and is visible to anyone who handles it — an identity-theft exposure with no compensating benefit.
   - Litigation trap: private right of action for "citizens" to sue the state or any county over compliance, with undefined standards, in a state already known for CEQA-style abuse. Election law expert Justin Levitt called it a "generic litigation trap." Plus high risk of federal Materiality Provision / NVRA challenges (as in Arizona's Mi Familia Vota).
   - Disparate impact: ~2.7 million Californians (11% of eligible voters) lack a driver's license; 13% have expired/outdated ones; disproportionately people of color, young, disabled, low-income. Married women who changed names face extra hurdles.
   - The citizenship-verification mandate has no workable data source (no comprehensive federal citizen database), risks erroneously flagging naturalized citizens, and would generate annual public "verification percentage" reports that could be weaponized politically.
   - It would write this into the state Constitution, where it's very hard to fix later (requires another statewide vote) — a poorly drafted, undefined standard locked into the constitution is bad governance regardless of one's view on voter ID.
   - Funding: $36.5M, two-thirds from out-of-state billionaire Richard Uihlein ($17M) plus Airbnb co-founder/White House official Joe Gebbia ($8M) — CalMatters reports national GOP donors view it as a test case for other swing states, not a California-specific reform.
   - Nearly every major California newspaper editorial board that examined it recommended NO (Sacramento Bee/McClatchy CA boards, SF Chronicle, LA Times, San Diego Union-Tribune, Mercury News/East Bay Times, Daily Californian). The Secretary of State, county registrars, and election administrators oppose it. Only a few (Pasadena Star-News) endorsed yes.
   - Polling: trailing consistently — PPIC Oct: 41% yes / 58% no; Berkeley IGS Sept: 39/52; Citrin-POLITICO Oct: 42/51. Even no-party-preference voters oppose by 13+ points.

Verdict: NO.

Let me do one last verification on the LA Times' editorial recommendation and whether there's any notable "yes" endorsement from a credible independent source, plus check the LA Times full guide entry for Prop 39 to make sure I have the complete picture. Also I want to double check the claim about "extended polling hours" in the Yes argument. And confirm the Nov 2026 election is unaffected (takes effect after certification).

Actually, I have enough. Let me do one final check on the LA Times editorial position and any strong "yes" case to be fair.

By The Editorial Board (https://www.pasadenastarnews.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)
PUBLISHED: October 15, 2026 at 3:13 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
A healthy democracy depends on both public participation and public trust. Without either, the system risks disaffection and loss of legitimacy.
California has made numerous moves in recent years to boost voter participation. From making it easier than ever to vote by mail to overly-liberal ballot harvesting laws, the Golden State has worked to optimize the public participation component of its election administration.
California has also maintained rising levels of public confidence in aspects of its elections. In 2017, just 47% of likely voters and 40% of adults either had “quite a lot of” or a “great deal of” confidence in how California counts votes, according to surveys by the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California. By 2024, those figures rose to 63% and 53%, respectively.
Lurking beneath (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/time-trends-all-adults-1024-corrected.pdf) those 2024 numbers were bigger concerns about election integrity than those figures suggest. The same survey found that 42% of adults and 43% of likely voters said they were “somewhat concerned” or “very concerned” that it’s “too easy for people who are not eligible to vote in California elections.”
Enter Proposition 39.
The proposal seeks to improve public confidence in elections with a simple rule: voters must present a government-issued ID when voting in person or include the last four digits of a government-issued ID that corresponds to identification used at the time of registration on the ballots they intend to mail in. For those who do not have such identification, the measure calls for free identification to be provided for voting.
It also requires election officials to maintain accurate voter registration lists and “use best efforts” to verify citizenship attestations. Finally, it directs regular audits by the State Auditor to ensure compliance with these rules and offer recommendations for how to improve election integrity.
There’s nothing radical about these recommendations. Thirty six states require voters to present some form of identification when voting. Such a requirement is commonplace around the world, including in Canada and Mexico. The logic of identification requirements is quite obvious: it’s simply another check to ensure that people are who they say they are when they vote. In fact, poll workers in California already ask (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/pdfs/trusted-info/trusted-info-voter-id-reg-requirements.pdf) first-time federal election voters who didn’t include an ID number at the time of registration for ID if they show up to the polls.
Opponents of voter identification requirements counter that requiring voters to provide identification at the polls is an unacceptable barrier to democratic participation. We disagree. If people can clear the “barrier” of presenting an ID to buy cigarettes or alcohol or use a credit card or get on an airplane, they can present ID to vote.
Opponents likewise counter that requiring voters to write the last four digits of their ID on their ballots introduces a failure point or privacy risk. We are sympathetic to privacy concerns, though such concerns would be more serious if the rule was to write the total ID number. And the failure point is real — what if voters write the wrong numbers? — but fixable. Ballots can be cured.
Research on the impact of such rules has been mixed over the years, with one review published by the National Bureau of Economic Research in 2019 finding (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5008639) that “strict identification laws are unlikely to have a meaningful impact on turnout or election outcomes.” Echoing this is an analysis published (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5008639) by the journal Research & Politics in December 2024 which found “no compelling evidence that strict voter ID laws consistently suppress or boost voter turnout. Rather, the modest and opposing impacts across contexts appear to net out to minimal aggregate effects on participation, consistent with research showing that electoral reforms often produce small equilibrium effects.”

2026 Election: California Ballot proposition endorsements from our opinion team could help make tough choices (https://www.pasadenastarnews.com/2026/10/20/2026-election-california-ballot-proposition-endorsements-from-our-opinion-team-could-help-make-tough-choices/)

Endorsement: No on Los Angeles County’s Measure A (https://www.pasadenastarnews.com/2026/10/08/endorsement-no-on-los-angeles-countys-measure-a/)
What could be the most controversial component of the measure is its mandate that election officials use “best efforts” to verify citizenship attestations using “government data.” The measure does not define these terms, thus giving the state and election officials room to figure out how to do that in the most reasonable manner possible. While this editorial board isn’t of the view that noncitizen voting is rampant, it doesn’t seem irrational to occasionally confirm people who attest to their citizenship actually are citizens.
If passed, we expect legal fights over the proposition as a whole and an adjustment period as it’s worked out. Combining the convenience of voting with basic verification isn’t voter suppression — it’s just common-sense governance. Vote Yes on Proposition 39.
